parole.significato: to be valid; to be correct or proper, to apply
parole.testo: From Old Swedish giælda, giælla, gælla, from Old Norse gjalda, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”). Under influence from Low German gelden, compare gälda. See also Icelandic gilda and Icelandic gildandi.
From earlier gälda, from Old Norse gelda (“to castrate”), from Proto-Germanic *galdijaną.
Inherited from Old Swedish gänger, from Old Norse gengr, from Proto-Germanic *gangiz. Compare Icelandic gengr, Norwegian Nynorsk gjeng and Danish gæng.

parole.significato: a deed, an action, a cost
parole.testo: From Old Swedish gærþ (“a deed, a cost, what must be done”), from Old Norse gørð, from Proto-Germanic *garwidō, related to the adjective *garwaz (“prepared, ready”). Related to göra (“to do”). Compare Icelandic gerð, Danish gærd.

parole.significato: gladly, happily, with keenness, (when synonymous with "gladly") willingly/readily
parole.testo: From Old Norse gjarna, from Proto-Germanic *gernô (“willingly, gladly”), the adverbial form of *gernaz (“willing”).
From the verb göra, from Old Norse gerning, gørning.
From Old Norse geispa.

From Old Swedish gæster, from Old Norse gestr, from Proto-Norse *ᚷᚨᛊᛏᛁᛉ (*gastiʀ), from Proto-Germanic *gastiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis. Cognates include Danish gæst and Norwegian Bokmål gjest.
From Old Swedish gā, from Old Norse gá, from Proto-Germanic *gāną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁-. Akin to English go.

From Old Norse gær.

From Old Swedish gās, from Old Norse gás, from Proto-Germanic *gans, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰh₂éns (“goose”). Cognate with English goose, German Gans, etc. In the other senses referring to the goose’s ability to float on water.

parole.significato: To have; to possess, or to have as a property; to come into possession of something concrete or abstract.

From Old Norse hafri, from Proto-Germanic *habrô, from Proto-Indo-European *kapro-.

parole.significato: A moor; an extensive waste land.

From Old Swedish heþin, from Old Norse heiðinn, from Proto-Germanic *haiþīnaz.

From Old Norse henni, dative of hón (“she”).

From Old Norse hertogi.

From Old Norse hinn. The noun, a noa-name, might have been formed by ellipsis of phrases such as hin håle and hin onde.

parole.significato: to have time, to have the time (for something), (sometimes, idiomatically) to make it
parole.testo: From Old Norse *hinna (“to reach”), from Proto-Germanic *hinþaną.

parole.significato: a film, a skin (very thin (often elastic) layer, on for example milk, but general)

Inherited from Old Swedish hion, from Old Norse hjón, hjún, hjú, from Proto-Germanic *hīwōnō.

From Old Swedish hiælmber, from Old Norse hjalmr (“helmet”), from Proto-Germanic *helmaz.
From Old Swedish hiælp, from Old Norse hjalp, hjǫlp.

parole.significato: a hero, a person (of any sex) of great bravery

parole.significato: hollow object; socket (like the shaft socket on a speartip)

From Old Swedish hoppa, huppa, from Old Norse hoppa, from Proto-Germanic *huppōną, from Proto-Indo-European *kewb- (“to bend; a bend, joint”).

parole.testo: From Old Swedish hōr, from Old Norse hór, from Proto-Germanic *hōrą, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“loved”). Related to English whore.
From Old Swedish hōra, from Old Norse hóra, from Proto-Germanic *hōrǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ros (“dear, loved”). Compare Danish hore, English whore, Dutch hoer, German Hure. Doublet of kär.
From Old Norse horn, from Proto-Norse ᚺᛟᚱᚾᚨ (horna), from Proto-Germanic *hurną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂-.
From Old Swedish hōsta, probably from the oblique case of Old Norse hósti, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstô.
From Old Swedish hōsta, from Old Norse hósta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōstōną.
From Old Swedish hōt n, from Old Norse hót n pl, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtō (“threat”), cognate with Gothic 𐍈𐍉𐍄𐌰 f (ƕōta). Related to *hwētaną (“to attack, stab”).

From Old Norse hóta, derived from the noun hót n pl (“threat”) (cf. Swedish hot). It has replaced an older (now obsolete) verb, höta, from Old Norse hœta, from Proto-Germanic *hwōtijaną, cognate with Danish høde (archaic), Gothic 𐍈𐍉𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (ƕōtjan).

parole.significato: a hoof (of an odd-toed ungulate, like a horse – compare klöv)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hōv, from Old Norse hófr, from Proto-Germanic *hōfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱoph₂ós. Cognate with Danish hov, English hoof, German Huf, Dutch hoef.
From Old Swedish hūþ, from Old Norse húð, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *kuHtis.

parole.significato: to strike with something sharp (to cut into pieces, sculpt, damage, or for any other purpose); to stab, to cut, to hew,…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hugga, from Old Norse hǫggva, from Proto-Germanic *hawwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kowH-.

parole.significato: a viper, an adder, especially the common European adder, Vipera berus
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hugormber, from Old Norse hǫggormr (“a serpent”). Equivalent to hugga + orm. Cognates include Icelandic höggormur (“a poisonous snake, a serpent”). Compare Old Norse hǫgg (“a stroke, a weapon's blow”) and ormr (“a snake, a serpent; a worm; a dragon”).

parole.significato: to go down into or be in a (half) sitting position; to squat, to crouch
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse húka. Cognate of German hocken, Dutch huiken. Doublet of hög.
From Old Swedish hulder, from Old Norse hollr, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌻𐌸𐍃 (hulþs), Icelandic hollur.

parole.significato: wood, forest (of any size); (or strictly) coppice
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish hult, from Old Norse holt (“wood”), from Proto-Germanic *hultą (“wood”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”). Cognate with English holt and German Holz. First attested in 1210–1216.

From Old Swedish humble, from Old Norse humli, humall, to a probable Proto-Germanic *humilô or thereof. Probably from Proto-Slavic *xъmelь Compare with Norwegian Bokmål humle, Faroese humli, humla, Icelandic humall.
From Old Norse humarr.

From Old Swedish hunder, from Old Norse hundr, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱwn̥tós, a variant of *ḱwṓ (“dog”). Masculine in Late Modern Swedish. Akin to Gothic 𐌷𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (hunds), English hound.
From Old Swedish hundraþ, from Old Norse hundrað, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).
From Old Norse hungr, from Proto-Germanic *hunhruz.
From Old Swedish hwaru, from a dative form of Old Norse hvar (“where”), see also var, Icelandic hvernug, Danish hvor.
From Old Swedish hūs, from Old Norse hús, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”).
From Old Norse húsbóndi, equivalent to hus + bonde. Cognate with English husband.
From Old Norse húskarl.

parole.significato: a hood, (UK) a bonnet, a (hard and removable) cover (e.g. over a car's engine), a lid
parole.testo: From Old Swedish huver, from Old Norse húfr. Cognate with Icelandic húfur.

parole.significato: a hood, a bonnet, a cap, a tea cosy, a (soft and removable) cover
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hūva, from Old Norse húfa, from Proto-Germanic *hūbǭ.
From Old Swedish hovuþ, from Old Norse hǫfuð, from Proto-Germanic *hafudą or *habudą, northern form of *haubudą, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-.
Related to hjälle (“scaffolding of poles”), itself from Old Norse hjallr. Alternatively to hålla (“to hold”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk hylle, Danish hylde, Icelandic hilla.
From Old Norse hylla, from Proto-Germanic *hulþijaną, from Proto-Germanic *hulþaz, (whence Swedish huld (“faithful, gracious, sweet”), Icelandic hollur (“loyal”)). Cognate with Icelandic hylla.
From Old Swedish hysa, from Old Norse hýsa, from Proto-Germanic *hūsijaną, equivalent to hus + -a. Cognate with Icelandic hýsa.

parole.significato: to blaspheme (express disdain for something considered holy)
parole.testo: Formed from the noun håd (“mockery”), from Old Swedish haþ, from Old Norse háð, from Proto-Germanic *hawiþą, related to *hauniz (“miserable”).

parole.significato: hence, herefrom, from here, away (from here)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæþan, from Old Norse héðan.

parole.significato: to stick (together), to attach, to adhere
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæpta, from Old Norse hepta, from Proto-Germanic *haftijaną. Cognate with Danish hæfte, Norwegian Norwegian hefta, Icelandic hepta, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐍆𐍄𐌾𐌰𐌽 (haftjan), Old Saxon heftian, hehtian, Middle Low German and Dutch hechten, and German heften.

parole.significato: heron; bird of the family Ardeidae
parole.testo: From the Old Norse hegri.
Inherited from Old Swedish hægger, from Old Norse heggr, from Proto-Germanic *hagô. Doublet of hage and häck. Compare English hedgeberry.
From Old Norse hæll, from Proto-Germanic *hanhilaz.

From Old Swedish *hæla, probably to an Old Norse *hæla (with cognate Danish hæle), ultimately to a Proto-Germanic *helaną. Doublet of hölja. Compare Old Swedish hæle (“hidden spot”), hæl (“death, underworld”). Cognate of German hehlen, Dutch helen (“to fence”).

parole.significato: half, one of two roughly equal parts
parole.testo: From Old Norse helft, from Proto-Germanic *halbiþō.

parole.significato: a more or less flat, often sloping section of rock surface
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hal, from Old Norse hallr, from Proto-Germanic *halluz.

parole.significato: to pour (cause (a liquid) to flow from a vessel by tilting it)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hælla, from Old Norse hella.
From Old Swedish hēlsa, from Old Norse heilsa, from Proto-Germanic *hailisōną, from *hailaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ilos.
From Old Swedish hämnd, from Old Norse hefnd, equivalent to hämna (“to avenge”) + -d.

parole.significato: to get, to fetch, to retrieve (go get and bring (back) somewhere)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæmta, from Old Norse heimta, from Proto-Germanic *haimatjaną.

parole.significato: away, hence (and often by implication to somewhere else)
parole.testo: From Old Norse héðan, with influence from Middle Low German hen (“away”), both ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *hiz (“this”).

parole.significato: to happen; chiefly what happens quickly or for a short time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hænda, from Old Norse henda, from Proto-Germanic *handijaną.

parole.significato: handy, crafty, skilled when it comes to practical things
parole.testo: From Old Norse hǫndugr, or more likely, from Middle Low German hendich; both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *handugaz.
From Old Swedish hængia, from Old Norse hanga, from Proto-Germanic *hanhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱenk-.

parole.significato: here; at this time or at this place
parole.testo: From Old Norse hér, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r.
From Old Norse herr, from Proto-Norse ᚺᚨᚱᛃᚨ (harja), from Proto-Germanic *harjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-.

parole.significato: a hundred; a court district in the Swedish countryside from medieval times until 1970
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæraþ, from Old Norse herað (“district; country”).

parole.significato: a lodging, a hostel, a shelter (affordable overnight lodging place)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hærbærghe, from Old Norse herbergi, from Middle Low German herberge. Cognate with English harbor.
Inherited from Old Swedish hærþa, from Old Norse herða, from Proto-Germanic *hardijaną.
From Old Swedish hæria, from Old Norse herja, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną. Derived from *harjaz (see här).
From Old Swedish härma, from Old Norse herma, from Proto-Germanic *harmijaną (“to repeat; to imitate”).

parole.significato: a horse; a large mammal, Equus caballus
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæster, from Old Norse hestr, from Proto-Germanic *hangistaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱanḱest-, *kankest-, see also German Hengst and Dutch hengst (“stallion”). The sense "heroin" is a calque from English "horse".
From Old Swedish hætta, Old Norse hetta, from Proto-Germanic *hattijǭ.

From Old Swedish hæfia, from Old Norse hefja, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyé-, from the root *kap- (“to seize”). Compare Danish hæve, Norwegian hevja, English heave, Dutch heffen, German heben. Doublet of hiva.

parole.significato: custom or practice that has long prevailed (and is therefore seen as legitimate), tradition, (as "av hävd") traditional…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hæfþ, from Old Norse hefð. Compare hävda.

parole.significato: to claim (with assurance, especially something that might be up for debate)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hefða.
From Old Swedish hogher, from Old Norse hugr, from Proto-Germanic *hugiz.

parole.significato: a hole (opening straight through or partway through something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hul, hol, from Old Norse hol, from Proto-Germanic *hulą, from Proto-Indo-European *kuH-, *kewH-.
From Old Swedish halda, halla, holda, holla, from Old Norse halda, from Proto-Germanic *haldaną. Further etymology uncertain; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).
From Old Swedish hār, from Old Norse hár, from Proto-Germanic *hērą, from Proto-Indo-European *keres- (“rough hair, bristle”).
From Old Swedish harþer, from Old Norse harðr, from Proto-Germanic *harduz, from Proto-Indo-European *kert-, *kret- (“strong, powerful”).

parole.significato: riches, treasures, bounty (especially bestowed upon someone by God, fate, fortune, or the like, sometimes abstract)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish hāva, from Old Norse hafa. Cognate of German Habe. Doublet of hava.
From Old Swedish hø̄, from Old Norse hey, from Proto-Germanic *hawją.

parole.significato: high; tall; reaching a great distance from the ground or being found high above it
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hø̄gher, from Old Norse haugr, from Proto-Germanic *haugaz, variant of *hauhaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-.
From Old Swedish hø̄gher, from Old Norse haugr, from Proto-Germanic *haugaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kewk-.

parole.significato: right (opposite of left; on the east side when facing north)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hǿgri, comparative of hǿgr (“easy, convenient”), from Proto-Germanic *hōgiz (“skilled”). Cognate with Icelandic hægri, Danish højre and Norwegian høyre.

parole.significato: height, altitude, elevation (distance above the ground or another reference)
parole.testo: Corresponds to Old Norse hæð, from Proto-Germanic *hauhiþō. Compare Norwegian Bokmål høyde, Dutch hoogte, Old High German hohida, Gothic hauhiþa, English height.
From Old Swedish hø̄ker, from Old Norse haukr, from Proto-Germanic *habukaz, probably ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize”).
From Old Swedish hylia, from Old Norse hylja, from Proto-Germanic *huljaną.

Derivative of hölja. From Old Swedish *hylster, from Old Norse hulstr, from Proto-Germanic *hulistrą. The suffix is rather unclear, but is also found in indigenous Old Swedish fiælster (“covering, hiding spot, secret location”) (to Old Norse fela (“hide”)), as well as alster (“offspring, product”) (

parole.significato: hen; in particular a female chicken
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hø̄na, from Old Norse hǿna, from Proto-Germanic *hōnijǭ, related to *hanjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kan- (“to sing”), *kana-.

parole.significato: chicken, fowl (bird of the genus Gallus, especially Gallus gallus domesticus)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish höns, from Old Norse hœns, hæns (“hens, poultry, fowl”, collectively).
From Old Swedish hø̄ra, from Old Norse heyra, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti.

parole.significato: a corner; the point where two converging lines meet; an angle, either external or internal.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hyrna, from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ.
From Old Norse hyrna, from Proto-Germanic *hurnijǭ.
From höst + -a, from Old Norse hausta. Cognate with Danish and Norwegian Bokmål høste.
From Old Swedish høfþinge, høfdhinger, høfþinger. From Old Norse hǫfðingi. Related to huvud (“head”).
From Old Swedish ī, īr, from Old Norse ír, variant of ér, from Proto-Germanic *jīz, variant of *jūz, from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs.

From Old Norse fjǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *ferudi (“last year”), from Proto-Indo-European *peruti (“last year”, literally “on the other side of a year”). The development from rð > l (originally /ɽ/) is characteristic of the traditional dialects of central and northern Sweden, compare e.g. vålnad, hi
From the Old Norse prepositional phrase í fjǫrð. See fjor for more.
From Old Swedish ī gār, from Old Norse í gær, í gjár (“yesterday”) (whence Icelandic í gær and Faroese í gjár).

From Old Swedish i løndom, cf. Danish i løndom. Originally a dative plural form of lønd (“secret”) (cf. lagom and stundom), from Old Norse leynd (“secret”). Ultimately from the same root as ljuga (“to lie”). The pronunciation has undergone analogy with words ending in -dom (“-dom”), changing the pit

parole.significato: used to signify that an action is done with intensity
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ī, from Old Norse í, from Proto-Germanic *in.
From Old Norse ek, from Proto-Norse ᛖᚲ (ek), -ᚲᚨ (-ka, “I”), Proto-Germanic *ek, *eka, *ik (“I”), from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm (“I”).
Clipping of i bland med (“in mixture with”), from Old Swedish i bland mæþ, from Old Norse í bland með.

parole.significato: yew (the tree Taxus baccata), more commonly known as idegran.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish idhe, ydhe (“yew”), from Old Norse *iði, from *iðja (“greenery”, literally “yew + collective suffix”), from an earlier *īṷiþia, from Proto-Germanic *īwiþia, *īhwiþia, a collective form of *īhwaz (“yew”) + *-iþia (“collective suffix”). Compare Swedish vide (“willow”), vidja (“withy,

Compound of ide (“yew”) + gran (“spruce”), from Old Swedish idhe, yew, from Old Norse *iði, from *iðja (“greenery”, literally “yew + collective suffix”), from an earlier *īṷiþia, from Proto-Germanic *īwiþia, *īhwiþia, a collective form of *īhwaz (“yew”) + *-iþia (“collective suffix”). Compare Swedis
From i + från, from Old Norse frá, from Proto-Germanic *fram (“from”), from Proto-Germanic *framaz (“forth, forward”).
From Old Swedish igil, from Old Norse *igla, from Proto-Germanic *egulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ógʷʰis (“snake”). Cognate with Icelandic igla, Danish igle, Norwegian igle and German Egel.
From Old Norse í gegn (“against”), from í (“in, on”) and gegn (“straight, direct”).
From Old Norse í gegnum.
From Old Norse í gær, í gjár (“yesterday”) (whence Icelandic í gær and Faroese í gjár). Akin to i + går.

parole.significato: as a race, by racing, competitively
parole.testo: From Old Norse kapp (“energy, zeal”), itself a variant of kamp (“battle”), probably via Middle Low German from Latin campus (“field, battlefield”).
From Old Swedish īlla, from Old Norse ílla, illa, adverb formation of Swedish ill, Old Swedish īlder, Old Norse íllr, illr. Related to English ill.

parole.significato: anger (a strong feeling of displeasure, hostility or antagonism towards someone or something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ilzka (noun), from Old Norse íllska, derivative of Old Swedish ilzker (“evil”, adjective), Old Norse *íllskr, to the same stem as ill (adjective), illa (adverb); Old Swedish ilder (adjective), Old Swedish illa (adverb); Old Norse íllr (adjective), ílla (adverb), from Proto-Germanic
From Old Swedish in, from Old Norse inn.
From Old Swedish ængin, from Old Norse engi, enginn, from einn (“one”) + -gi (privative suffix).
From Old Norse inngangr, from Proto-Germanic *inngangaz. Equivalent to in- + gång.
From Old Swedish innan, from Old Norse innan, from Proto-Norse ᛁᚾᚨᚾᚨ (inana), from Proto-Germanic *innanē.
From Old Swedish inne, from Old Norse inni.

parole.significato: Irish (pertaining to Ireland, in particular Celtic aspects of its culture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish irsker, from Old Norse írskr. Cognate of Danish irsk, German irisch, English Irish.
From Old Swedish is, from Old Norse íss, from Proto-Germanic *īsą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eyH-.

parole.significato: lard, grease; a solid but soft fat from the intestines of certain animals
parole.testo: From Old Swedish īster, from Old Norse ístr, from Proto-Germanic *instraz (“intestine”).

parole.significato: apart, asunder; into two or more pieces
parole.testo: From i + sär, which itself is derived from Old Norse sér. Cognate with Danish især, Norwegian Nynorsk især.

parole.significato: The letter "I" in the Swedish spelling alphabet
parole.testo: From Old Norse Ívarr.
From Old Norse já, from Proto-Germanic *ja.
From Old Swedish iak, jæk, from Old Norse jak (compare Old West Norse ek), from Proto-Norse ᛖᚲ (ek), from Proto-Germanic *ek, from Proto-Indo-European *eǵh₂óm.
From Late Old Swedish iagha, from Early Old Swedish iægha, from Old Norse jaga, from Middle Low German jāgen, from Old Saxon *jagōn, from Proto-West Germanic *jagōn.

parole.significato: yes; used as a disagreement to a negative statement or a negatively phrased question (has no English equivalent, but eq…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish iū, from Old Norse jaur.

parole.significato: earth, soil; a rock- or sand-based unconsolidated material in which land plants grow
parole.testo: From Old Swedish iorþ, from Old Norse jǫrð, from Proto-Germanic *erþō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁er-.

From Old Swedish iūl, from Old Norse jól, from Proto-Germanic *jehwlą. First attested in the late 13th century. Cognate with English Yule, Danish jul, Estonian jõulud, Finnish joulu, Faroese jól, Icelandic jól, Norwegian jul, and Scots Yule.

parole.significato: an udder (part of domestic milk-giving animal that expresses milk)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish iūwer, iūver (Early Old Swedish), iūger, iūgher (Late Old Swedish), from Old Norse júr, júgr, from Proto-Germanic *euduraz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ewHdʰ-r̥- (“udder”).

From Old Swedish iæmpn, from Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz. Compare Danish jævn, Norwegian Bokmål jevn, Norwegian Nynorsk jamn, Faroese javnur, Icelandic jafn, English even, Dutch even, effen, German eben.
From Old Swedish iæmnaþer, from Old Norse jafnaðr.
From Old Swedish iæmpnt (“even”, adjective), neuter of iæmpn, from Old Norse jafn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz.

parole.significato: a girl (female child or young woman)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse genta, from gant (“joke, foolery”). Cognate with Norwegian jente.

parole.significato: night (particularly in spring or autumn) during which temperature unexpectedly drops below 0 °C
parole.testo: Possibly compound of järn (“iron”) + natt. First part might be from Old Norse hjarn (“hard frozen snow”). Cognate of Norwegian Nynorsk jarnnatt.
From Old Swedish iärpe, from Old Norse jarpi, from Old Norse jarpr (“brown”), from Proto-Germanic *erpaz (“light brown”).

From Old Swedish iærver, from Old Norse jarfr, from Proto-Norse ᛖᚱᚨᚠᚨᛉ (erafaʀ), of debated origin. Cognate with Faroese jarvur, Norwegian Nynorsk jerv & Norwegian Bokmål jerv, and possibly related to Old Norse jarpr (“brown”), Old English eorp (“brown; dark, dusky”), from Proto-Germanic *erpaz (“li
From Old Swedish iæster, from Old Norse jǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *jestuz, from Proto-Indo-European *yes- (“to boil, to foam”).

parole.significato: jotun; a mythical humanoid creature, originally human-sized but later associated with great size
parole.testo: From, iætti, from Old Norse *iætti, byform of Old Norse jǫtunn, from Proto-Germanic *etunaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-. Doublet of (dialectal) jutul, juttul, jottel (“the devil; clever handy man, trixter, sly fox”); from Old Swedish *iatul, alternative form of iætun (“giant; jotun”); also borr

parole.significato: disqualification, challenge (judge's interest in the result of the case for which they should not be allowed to sit)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish iæf (“doubt”), from Old Norse ef (“doubt”), from Proto-Germanic *jabą, *ibą, whence Proto-Germanic *jabai (“if”), whence Icelandic ef (“if”) and Old English ġif (“if”).

parole.significato: a cable (conductor – heavily insulated wire, fiber-optic cable, network cable, etc. – same as in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kabel (“heavy rope”), kabbla (plural) (15th c.), from Old Norse kabill (14th c.), by some merit a derivative of kabb- (“spool, roll”) + -ill (agent suffix), related to kafli (“roll; handle, swordhilt”), but also a derivative of Old Northern French cable, Occitan câble, from Late Lat
From Old Norse kaggi.
From Old Swedish kaka, from Old Norse kaka, from Proto-Germanic *kakǭ (“cake”), from Proto-Indo-European *gog- (“ball-shaped object”).

parole.significato: lacking its natural covering; bare, without hair or vegetation or leaves or the like
parole.testo: From or related to Old Norse *kǫlr, from Proto-Germanic *kalwaz (“bare, bald”).
From Old Swedish kalder, kaller, from Old Norse kaldr, from Proto-Germanic *kaldaz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gel-.

parole.significato: a calling (strong urge to dedicate oneself to something, often an occupation felt to have a higher purpose)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kall. Related to Swedish and Old Norse verb kalla.

parole.significato: to call, denote, refer to; to give as a name
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kalla, from Old Norse kalla, from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną.

From Old Swedish kalver, from Old Norse kalfr (“calf”), from Proto-Germanic *kalbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷolbʰo- (“womb, animal young”). Compare Norwegian and Danish kalv, Icelandic kálfur, Dutch kalf, German Kalb, English calf.

From Old Swedish kamber, from Old Norse kambr, cognate with Danish kam and Dutch kam. That in turn derived from Proto-Germanic *kambaz, whence also Old English camb (English comb), Old High German kamb (German Kamm). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵómbʰos (“tooth (animate)”), whence also Ancie

parole.significato: camel (especially the Bactrian camel, Camelus bactrianus)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kamel, from Late Old Norse kamell, from Latin camelus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos, “camel”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *gamal-.

parole.significato: to comb (to groom the hair with a toothed implement)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kamba, replaced older umlauted form kæmba under influence by the noun kamber (“comb”), from Old Norse kemba, from Proto-Germanic *kambijaną. Compare Danish kæmme, Norwegian kjemme, Icelandic kemba.
From late Old Norse kamarr, from Latin camera (“room, chamber”) or camara, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “vault”).

parole.significato: a (large) vessel with a handle and spout; a jug, a pot
parole.testo: From Old Norse kanna.
From Old Norse ker, from Proto-Germanic *kazą.

parole.significato: a “real man”, a capable man, a full grown man (compare kraftkarl (“strongman”), karlaktig (“in manly fashion”))
parole.testo: From Late Old Swedish karl, kar, kall, from Old Norse karl (attested on runestones as ᚴᛅᚱᛚ (karl)), from Proto-Norse *ᚲᚨᚱᛁᛚᚨᛉ (*karilaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *karilaz.

parole.significato: a frame (for a door or window)
parole.testo: From Old Norse karmr, which is related to krókr (“hook”).

parole.significato: karve; a multipurpose intermediate size Viking longship
parole.testo: Derived from Old Swedish karve, from Old Norse karfi.

parole.significato: a pyre, a bonfire (usually a loose heap of brushwood, branches, and the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kasi (“collection”), from or related to Old Norse kǫs (“pile, heap”).
From Old Norse kast, verbal noun to kasta (“throw”).

parole.significato: to throw (make an object fly through the air)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kasta, from Old Norse kasta, from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), of unknown origin. Cognate with Faroese, Icelandic, Norwegian Nynorsk kasta, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål kaste and English cast.

From the older form kavle, from Old Swedish kafle, kafli, from Old Norse kafli, from Proto-Germanic *kablaz (“round piece of wood”). Cognate to Norwegian Nynorsk kjevle, Norwegian Bokmål kjevle, Icelandic kefli.
From Old Swedish kiþ, from Old Norse kið, from Proto-Germanic *kidją‚ from Proto-Indo-European *gidʰ-.
From Old Swedish kiþlinger, from Old Norse kiðlingr, equivalent to kid (now fawn, before all baby animals); -ling (diminutive suffix).
From Old Norse kinn, from Proto-Germanic *kinnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénu- (“cheek”). Compare Danish kind, Norwegian and Icelandic kinn, German Kinn, Dutch kin, English chin.
From Old Norse kista.

parole.significato: a cauldron, a kettle (large cooking vessel)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ketill, from Proto-Germanic *katilaz, from Late Latin catillus.
From Old Swedish kitla, from Old Norse kitla, from Proto-Germanic *kitilōną, frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *kitōną (“to tickle”), from Proto-Indo-European *geid- (“to stick, jab, tickle”).
Inherited from Old Norse kífa, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.
Inherited from Old Norse kífa, from Proto-Germanic *kībaną.
From klappa (“to clap”), from Old Norse klappa, from Proto-Germanic *klappōną.

Inherited from Old Swedish klen, from Old Norse klénn, from Middle Low German klên, klêne, from Old Saxon klēni, from Proto-Germanic *klainiz (“clear, pure”), from Proto-Indo-European *g(e)lēi- (“gleaming”), from *gel- (“to gleam”). Doublet of klenod and klenät.

parole.significato: a rift, cleft or gap in rock
parole.testo: From Old Norse kleif.
From Old Norse kláði.

parole.significato: to cut with scissors, shears, or the like (cut with two blades or the like in a snipping motion), to clip (compare skär…
parole.testo: From Old Norse klippa, klyppa.

parole.significato: to take one or more big steps, to step, to stride
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klīva, from Old Norse klífa, from Proto-Germanic *klībaną.
From Old Norse kló, from Proto-Germanic *klawō.

parole.significato: clock, watch; an instrument used to measure or keep track of time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish klockæ, from Old Norse klokka, from Late Latin clocca, probably of Celtic origin, from Proto-Celtic *klokkos (“bell”) (compare Welsh cloch, Irish clog), from Proto-Indo-European *klēg-, *klōg- (onomatopoeia).
From Old Swedish kloker, from Old Norse klókr, from Middle Low German klôk, from Old Saxon *klōk, from Proto-Germanic *klōkaz. Cognate to German klug.
Inherited from Old Swedish klokskaper, from Old Norse klókskapr. By surface analysis, klok + -skap. Cognate of Danish klogskab.

parole.significato: monastery (place of residence for members of a religious community)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kloster, kløster, from Old Norse klaustr.
From Old Norse klubba with uncertain origin. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk klubbe and English club. Probably related to Danish kølle and Norwegian Nynorsk kolv.
From Old Swedish klūter, from Old Norse klútr, from Proto-Germanic *klūtaz. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål klut, Danish klud, English clout (“cloth”), Old English clūt. Compare with origin for klot.

parole.significato: a clove; a separate bulb of a garlic
parole.testo: From Old Norse kluft, klyft, from Proto-Germanic *kluftiz.
From Old Swedish klȳva, from Old Norse kljúfa, from Proto-Germanic *kleubaną (“to cleave, split”), from Proto-Indo-European *glewbʰ-.

parole.significato: to hatch; to emerge from an egg
parole.testo: From Old Norse klekja.
From Old Swedish klæþi, from Old Norse klæði, borrowed from Old Frisian klāth, klēth or Old English clāþ, clǣþ, from Proto-Germanic *klaiþą (“garment”). Cognate with English cloth and German Kleid.
From Old Swedish klædhe, from Old Norse klæði. Compare kläde and English cloth.
Inherited from Old Swedish klēngia, from Old Norse klengja, from Proto-Germanic *klangijaną. Doublet of klunga.
From Old Norse klettr (“crag, cliff”). Doublet of klint.
From Old Swedish klā, from Old Norse klá, from Proto-Germanic *klawjaną. Doublet of klia, klösa, klo, and klåda.

parole.significato: to load an animal with saddlebags
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish klyfia, from Old Norse klyfja. Cognate of Norwegian Bokmål kløvje. Doublet of klyva.
From Old Norse knappr, from Proto-Germanic *knappô, *knappa-, which is perhaps related to *knappō (“knob, boy”).
From Old Swedish knīver, from Old Norse knífr (“knife”), from Proto-Germanic *knībaz, from Proto-Indo-European *gneybʰ-.
From Old Swedish knōe, from Old Norse knúi, from Proto-Germanic *knūwan. See also Danish kno; further Swedish knoka, German Knochen, Dutch knook, knokkel, English knuckle.

parole.significato: a knot (loop, of for example a piece of string)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish knūter from Old Norse knútr, from Proto-Germanic *knuttô, *knudô (compare *knuttan-, whence English knot). Originally of corner joints of log cabins in (sense 2).
From Old Swedish knyta, from Old Norse knýta, from Proto-Germanic *knuttijaną, related to *knuttô.
From Old Norse kné, from Proto-Germanic *knewą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu (“knee”).
From Old Swedish knodha, from Old Norse knoða, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną, compare dialectal knö.

parole.significato: to crowd, to jostle, to squeeze
parole.testo: From knå, a dialectal short form of standard Swedish knåda (“to knead”), with western Swedish vowel fronting /oː/ > /œː/, sometimes represented in dialectal writing with a circumflex ⟨ô⟩, compare gôr-. From Old Swedish knodha, from Old Norse knoða, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną.
From Old Norse ko, from East Old Norse ko, from Proto-Germanic *kōz.
From Old Norse kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷol-, from *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”).
From Old Swedish koma, from Old Norse koma, from Proto-Germanic *kwemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem-. Etymology 1 sense 3 is probably a semantic loan from English come.

From Old Swedish kona, kuna (“woman, wife, concubine”) (genitive plural kvinna, kvænna), from Old Norse kona, from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ. Feminine in Late Modern Swedish. Doublet of kvinna. Akin to English quean.
From Old Swedish konunger, from Old Norse konungr (“king”), from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”).
From Old Swedish kop, from Old Norse koppr, probably from Middle Low German kop, from Proto-West Germanic *kopp, from Proto-Germanic *kuppaz.

parole.significato: chancel, choir (space around the altar in a church)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kor, from Old Norse kórr, from Latin chorus, from Ancient Greek χορός (khorós).

From Old Swedish korver, presumably from Old Norse kurfr, from Proto-Germanic *kurbiz. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kurv (with dialectal variants like korv and kørv), and English kerf. Attested since the first half of the 15th century.
From Old Norse kussa (“cow”); see ko (“cow”). Cognate with Icelandic kusa (“cow”).

parole.significato: diet, food (The food and beverage a person or animal habitually consumes, or food more generally)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kostr, from Middle Low German kost, koste.
From Old Norse kosta, from Middle Low German [Term?], from Latin constare.

parole.significato: a koster (type of wide sailboat from Bohuslän)
parole.testo: From Koster, also called Kosteröarna (the Koster islands), an archipelago in northern Bohuslän, known as the Koster Islands in English. The name is of uncertain origin, possibly Old Norse kostir (“eating place”), referring to bountiful fishing around the islands, from kostr (“choice, goods, food”).
From Old Swedish krabba, krabbe, from Old Norse krabbi, from Proto-Germanic *krabbô, from Proto-Indo-European *grobʰ- (“to crawl, scratch”). See also kräfta (“crayfish”).

parole.significato: to scratch the surface (layer) of something (with claws or fingers)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krapsa, one of many derivations related to Old Norse grafa (“to dig, bury”).

parole.significato: force (similar senses to English, though less often of groups of people)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krapter, from Old Norse kraptr, krǫptr, from Proto-Germanic *kraftuz.

From Old Swedish kraghi, from Old Norse kragi and Middle Low German krage, from Proto-Germanic *kragô (“throat”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrogʰ-. Related to Swedish kräva (“crop of a bird”); compare English craw, crag (“crop of a bird”).

parole.significato: a pitiful (and weak, in some sense) person or animal (arousing pity or contempt); a wretch
parole.testo: From the earlier sense of "rod," "gnarled wood," ultimately related to Old Norse krókr (“hook”).

parole.significato: A merchandise, commodities, small and cheap products sold to consumers; trash (useless merchandise).
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kram, from Old Norse kram, from Middle Low German kräm (“fine cloth; also used for merchant tents, thus later a synonym for merchandise”), probably ultimately of Slavic origin; see German Kram. Related to Danish kram, Icelandic kram.
From Old Swedish krama, from Old Norse kremja.

From late Old Norse kranz, from Middle Low German kranz, from Middle High German kranz, from Old High German kranz, probably altered from krenz, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *kringaz (“circle, ring”).

parole.significato: to make a sound (kras) like something brittle breaking (for example glass)
parole.testo: From Old Norse *krasa, ultimately of imitative origin. Compare Swedish krossa (“to crush”), English crush, crash, craw, crow. A related term is potentially Old Swedish kraza (“to quarrel, to fight”). A cognate is English craze.
From Old Norse krǫf f, from Proto-Germanic *krafō, related to Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”).

From Old Norse krafla (compare Danish kravle (“to crawl, creep”), Swedish kräla (“to creep, crawl”)), from Proto-Germanic *krablōną (compare Saterland Frisian krabbelje, Dutch krabbelen, German Low German krabbeln, German krabbeln), frequentative of *krabbōną (“to scratch, scrape”). Compare also Sat
From Old Norse kringr, originally "turn or go about in circles," from Proto-Germanic *kringaz.

parole.significato: a kringle (type of pastry, Nordic variety of pretzel)
parole.testo: From Old Norse kringla
From Old Swedish kristin, from Old Norse kristinn, from Middle Low German kristen or Old English cristen, from Latin Christianus, from Greek χρῑστιᾱνός (christianós).

parole.significato: a hook (rod bent into a curved shape)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krōker, from Old Norse krókr, from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz.

parole.significato: a body (of a human, whether living or dead, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kropper, from Old Norse kroppr (“body”), from Proto-Germanic *kruppaz, from Proto-Indo-European *grewb-.

From Old Norse krús, from Middle Low German krus, kros, of uncertain ultimate origin, but Pokorny proposes an ultimate derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend”), similar to Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“something bent, crooked”), *krukjō (“staff”).
From Old Swedish krympa, from Old Norse krimpa (Compare Old West Norse kreppa), from Proto-Germanic *krimpaną.

From Old Swedish krȳpa, from Old Norse krjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *kreupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“turn, wind”). Compare Norwegian krype, Danish krybe, Icelandic krjúpa, English creep, Dutch kruipen.

parole.significato: to tense the muscles of the abdomen in order to expel something (usually feces or a baby); to push, to bear down
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krȳsta, from Old Norse *krjósta, from Proto-Germanic *kreustaną (“to grind”).
From Old Swedish krängia, from Old Norse krinkr, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz (“circle, ring”).

From Old Swedish kræva, kræve, from a Old Norse *kravi, of uncertain origin. See Old Norse kragi. Cognate of Danish krave (“collar, crop of a bird”), English craw (“crop of a bird”), potentially also Swedish krage.
From Old Swedish kræfia, from Old Norse krefja, from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną or Proto-Germanic *krabjaną. Cognate with Danish kræve, Norwegian Bokmål kreve, Old English crafian and English crave.

parole.significato: crow, especially hooded crow, Corvus cornix
parole.testo: From Old Swedish krāka, from Old Norse kráka, from Proto-Germanic *krakǭ, a derivative of *krakōną, from Proto-Indo-European *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”). Cognate to German krähe, English crow.
From Old Swedish kodde, from Old Norse koddi, from Proto-Germanic *kuddô, from Proto-Indo-European *gewt-.
From Old Norse kokkr, from Proto-Germanic *kukkaz. Cognate with English cock.

parole.significato: a small ball made of earthenware, glass (marble) or a similar hard material; of steel in a ball bearing; sphere
parole.testo: From Old Norse kúla (“lump, swelling”), with the meaning of "sphere" influenced by Middle Low German kule (“depression, bulge”) and German Kugel (“ball, sphere, bullet”).
From Old Norse kollr, from Proto-Germanic *kullaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish kumbel, from Old Norse kumbl, from Proto-Germanic *kumblą.
From contraction of konung, from Old Swedish konunger, from Old Norse konungr, from Proto-Germanic *kuningaz (“king”).
From Old Swedish kunna, from Old Norse kunna, from Proto-Germanic *kunnaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵneh₃-.

parole.significato: knowledgeable, especially in a way that makes one competent (within a particular area); having (great) knowledge, know-…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kunnogher, from Old Norse kunnigr, equivalent to kunna + -ig. Cognate of German kundig, Dutch kundig, Danish kyndig.

parole.significato: a rumble, a slight rumbling sound, usually from the stomach
parole.testo: From the verb kurra (“to rumble”), from Old Norse kurr (“growling”), of imitative origin. The Norse word was borrowed into Middle English curre (“aggressive dog”).
Uncertain; possibly a variant of kunta, from Old Norse kunta.
From Old Swedish qval, from Old Norse kvǫl, from Proto-Germanic *kwalō. Cognate of German Qual, Dutch kwaal, Old English cwalu. Compare origin of kvälja.
From Old Norse kvirr, kyrr, from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz.
From Old Swedish quaster, from Old Norse *kvǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *kwastuz.
From Old Swedish qviþer (“belly, stomach, womb”), from Old Norse kviðr, from Proto-Germanic *kweþuz. Cognate with Icelandic kviður, Old English cwiþ, Gothic 𐌵𐌹𐌸𐌿𐍃 (qiþus).

From Old Swedish qvikker, qviker, from Old Norse kvikr (whence also Norwegian Bokmål kvikk, Norwegian Nynorsk kvik, Icelandic kvikur and Faroese kvikur), from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz, whence also English quick. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).
From Old Swedish qvikna, from Old Norse kvikna, from Proto-Germanic *kwiknaną.
From Old Norse kvíga.
From Old Swedish kvinna, from Runic Swedish kuino, from Old Norse kvæna, from kván (“wife”), from Proto-Germanic *kwenǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷḗn. Cognate with English queen.

parole.significato: feminine (having the qualities associated with a woman)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish qvinliker, qvinzliker, from Old Norse kvennsligr and kvennligr. Akin to kvinna + -lig.
From Old Norse kvistr.
From Old Swedish kvæþa, from Old Norse kveða, from Proto-Germanic *kweþaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-. Cognate with English quoth, Icelandic kveða.

parole.significato: lay, poem, song (used mostly in reference to Old Norse poetry)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kvæþe, from Old Norse kvæði, from Proto-Germanic *kwēþiją.
From Old Swedish qvælia, from Old Norse kvelja, from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną. Compare Old Armenian կեղ (keł).
From Old Swedish quæld, qvælder, from Old Norse kveld, from Proto-Germanic *kwildiz, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelH-.
From Old Swedish kyklinger, from Old Norse kjúklingr.

parole.significato: to chill, to cool, to refrigerate; to lower the temperature of something
parole.testo: From Old Norse kœla, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną.

From Old Swedish kyrkia, kirkia, from Old Norse kirkja, from Old English cirice, from Late Proto-West Germanic *kirikā, from Byzantine Greek κυριακόν (δόμα) (kuriakón (dóma), literally “Lord's (house)”), from Ancient Greek κύριος (kúrios, “lord”).
From Old Swedish kus, kos, from Old Norse koss, from Proto-Germanic *kussaz. Cognate with English kiss, German Kuss, Icelandic koss.

parole.significato: to kiss passionately or with great affection (compare with pussa), to snog (UK)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kyssa, from Old Norse kyssa, from Proto-Germanic *kussijaną.

parole.significato: a jaw or (open) mouth of an animal (especially one with a powerful bite)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kiæpter, from Old Norse kjaptr. Cognate with Danish kæft, Norwegian kjeft, Icelandic kjaftur, and Faroese kjaftur.
Inherited from Old Norse kjalki.

parole.significato: a source (of information, or other things)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kælda, from Old Norse kelda.
From Old Norse ketlingr, equivalent to katt + -ling with umlaut. Compare Icelandic kettlingur and Danish killing.
From Old Swedish kænna, from Old Norse kenna, from Proto-Germanic *kannijaną.

parole.significato: lore (achieved knowledge), learning(s), teaching(s) (consumed education, experience), doctrine
parole.testo: By surface analysis, känna + -dom, the lead being causative of kunna (“to know”). From Old Swedish kænnedomber (attested since the 15th c.), from Old Norse kennidómr.
From Old Swedish kænsla, from Old Norse kensla.
From Old Swedish käpper, from Old Norse keppr.

From Old Swedish kær, from Old Norse kærr, from Old Northern French ker, kier, quer (Old French chier, cher), from Latin cārus (“dear”), from Proto-Italic *kāros, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂- (“to desire, to wish”). Doublet of hora.
From Old Swedish kärling, from Old Norse kerling.
Inherited from Old Swedish käril, from Old Norse kerald (“container”), from Proto-Germanic *kazą. Doublet of kar.

parole.significato: love (strong affection, romantically or more generally, like in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kærleker, from Old Norse kærleikr, equivalent to kär + -lek.

parole.significato: a seed (of a fruit, nut, berry, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kiærne, from Old Norse kjarni, from Proto-Germanic *kernô (“core, kernel”). Cognate with Icelandic kjarni, German Kern, Dutch kern, Luxembourgish Kär.

parole.significato: a churn (a vessel used for churning, especially for producing butter)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kerna, from Old Norse kirna, from Proto-Germanic *kernǭ. Cognate with Icelandic kirna, English churn, German Karn, Dutch karn, West Frisian tsjerne.

From Old Norse kjarr (“copsewood, underbrush, bushes, scrub”), from Proto-Germanic *kerzą, *kerzuz (“scrub, bushes”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵers- (“to turn, bend, twist”). Cognate with Danish kær (“brushwood, undergrowth, scrub”), Norwegian Bokmål kjerr, Norwegian Nynorsk kjørr (“thicket”), Icel
From Old Swedish kärling, from Old Norse kerling. Equivalent to karl + -ing.

From Old Norse þjarfr, from Proto-Germanic *þerbaz. Arguably related, more distantly, to Icelandic stjarfi (“tetanus”), German sterben (“to die”), Russian терпкий (terpkij, “astringent, tart, acerbic”).

From Old Swedish kærve, from Old Norse kerfi, kjarf, likely from Proto-Germanic *kerbą, a derivation of Proto-Germanic *krebô (“basket, bucket”). Related to karva, korv, karm. Compare Middle Dutch kerven, German kerben, Old English ceorfan. Cognate with Icelandic kerfi (“system”), Faroese kervi (“sh

Inherited from Old Swedish qvāþa, kādha, kode, from Old Norse kváða. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk kvae and Icelandic kvoða. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷet-, whence also English cud, German Kitt and Sanskrit जतु (jatu).

parole.significato: cabbage; edible plants of the species Brassica oleracea; more generally any plant in the genus Brassica
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kāl, from Old Norse kál, from Old English cawel, caul, cāl, from Latin caulis, from Ancient Greek καυλός (kaulós, “stem”), from Proto-Indo-European *kaw(ǝ)l or *kowos.

parole.significato: a sudden blow of cold wind; a chill or a shiver
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse kári (“gust of wind”).

From Old Swedish kāter, from Old Norse kátr, from Proto-Germanic *kanhtaz. Cognate with Danish kåd, Norwegian Bokmål kåt and Norwegian Nynorsk kåt. Possibly also related to Latin gaudeō (“to rejoice”).
From Old Swedish kiøl, kiol, from Old Norse kjǫlr, from Proto-Norse *kelu-, from Proto-Germanic *keluz.

parole.significato: cold (normally outdoors and intense, like at least below freezing (0°C); also of the sensation)
parole.testo: Derived from the adjective kall, both from Old Norse kaldr.

parole.significato: an oast, a kiln; a room or building for drying malt and hop
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kølna, from Old Norse kylna. Cognate with Danish kølle, English kiln, Old English cyln, ultimately from Latin Latin culina (“portable stove”). The verb has been used since 1706 (to kindle a fire) and 1873 (to dry malt).

From Old Swedish køn, kyn, from Old Norse kyn, from Proto-Germanic *kunją, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁- (“to produce”). Cognate with English kin, Danish køn, Norwegian kjønn, Icelandic kyn, Dutch kunne, Gothic 𐌺𐌿𐌽𐌹 (kuni), and the borrowed Finnish word kunnia.

From Old Swedish kø̄pa, from Old Norse keypa, kaupa, from Proto-Germanic *kaupijaną, *kaupōną (“to buy, trade”), from *kaupô (“innkeeper, merchant”), Latin caupo (“innkeeper, shopkeeper, tradesman”), caupōnor (“to trade, haggle”). Cognate with Danish købe, Norwegian kjøpe, German kaufen, Dutch kopen

parole.significato: a market town, a small town (official status as a smaller town in Sweden before 1971, in Finland before 1977)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kø̄punger, from Old Norse kaupangr.
From Old Swedish kø̄ra, from Old Norse keyra (“to drive, fling, toss”), from Proto-Germanic *kaurijaną, *karjaną (“to turn, sweep”). More at cair.
From Old Swedish køt, kiøt, from Old Norse kjǫt, from Proto-Germanic *ketwą. Cognate with Danish kød, Norwegian kjøtt, kjøt, Faroese kjøt, Icelandic kjöt.

parole.significato: barn, an unheated building used for storage of hay and similar.
parole.testo: From Old Norse hlaða f.
From Old Norse hlaða, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kleh₂-. See also lada (“barn”).

parole.significato: law (the body of rules established in a community by its authorities)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lagh, from Old Norse lǫg. Cognate with Danish lov, Norwegian lov, English law. Related to Old Norse leggja “to define”.

parole.significato: a water-based solution of sugar, salt and/or other spices; e.g. brine
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lagher, from Old Norse lǫgr, from Proto-Germanic *laguz, from Proto-Indo-European *lókus. Cognate with Latin lacus.

parole.significato: a team, a workgroup (any group of people involved in the same activity, especially sports or work)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lagh, from Old Norse lag. Derived from Old Norse leggja (“to lay”) or liggja (“to lie”).
From Old Norse lagg (“barrel stave, split piece of wood”), from Proto-Germanic *lawwd, from Proto-Indo-European *lewH- (“to sever, cut apart, loosen”).

parole.significato: legal (something which is allowed or prescribed by law)
parole.testo: lag + -lig, from Old Norse lǫgligr. Cognate with Icelandic löglegur.

parole.significato: a chief judge of a tingsrätt (“district court”) and länsrätt (“county administrative court”)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish laghman, from Old Norse lǫgmaðr. By surface analysis, lag + man.
From Old Swedish lakan, from Late Old Norse lak, lakan, from Old Saxon lakan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“sheet, cloth”).
From Old Norse laki.

parole.significato: lame, unable to move any limbs
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lamber, from Old Norse lami, from Proto-Germanic *lamaz.
From Old Swedish lamb, from Old Norse lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁l̥h₁onbʰos.
From Old Norse lampi, from Middle Low German lampe, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás, “torch”).

parole.significato: a country, a land (independent political entity)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish land, from Old Norse land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).
From Old Norse lenda, derived from the noun land.

parole.significato: province, region (chiefly about the Scandinavian countries and e.g. Czech Republic)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish landskap, from Old Norse landskapr. Equivalent to land + -skap.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: a patch, a piece of any flexible material, used to cover a hole in something; such as a piece of fabric used over a hol…
parole.testo: From Old Norse leppr, from Proto-Germanic *lappaz, *lappô (“rag, cloth”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Compare Icelandic leppur, Danish lap, Middle Dutch lappe, Old High German lappa, German Lappen (“patch”), Lithuanian lopas (“patch, piece”) and Latvi

parole.significato: habit which is difficult to get rid of, vice
parole.testo: From Old Swedish laster (Old Icelandic lǫstr), from Old Norse löstr, from the root of Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to reproach, blame”), see also Old High German lastar (“vice”).
From Old Swedish later, from Old Norse latr, from Proto-Germanic *lataz, from Proto-Indo-European *lē(y)d-.

From Old Norse lax, from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz. The 1000 SEK sense probably refers to the salmon color of old 1000 SEK banknotes. Compare the similarly themed older slang skäring, from skär (“pink”); räka (“prawn”); tegel (“brick”); and röding (“char”), from röd (“red”); all referring to the red-pi
From Old Swedish lēia, lea, from Old Norse hlæja (“to laugh”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną.
Inherited from Old Swedish lēþer, from Old Norse leiðr, from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂leyt-.

parole.significato: joint; the part of a limb where it can bend; such as a knee or a wrist; phalanx
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish liþer, from Old Norse liðr, from Proto-Germanic *liþuz.

parole.significato: track, route or way, along which one may walk, go by bicycle or drive a motor vehicle
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish lēþ, from Old Norse leið, from Proto-Germanic *laidō.

parole.significato: to (gently) lead; to guide, to conduct
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lēþa, from Old Norse leiða, from Proto-Germanic *laidijaną.
From Old Norse liðugr, from Proto-Germanic *liþugaz.
Inherited from Old Norse leiðangr.
From Old Swedish legha, lægha, from Old Norse lega, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną (“to lie; to rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”). Doublet of lager and läger.
From Old Swedish lēgha, from Old Norse leiga (“hire, rent, pay”), from Proto-Germanic *laigǭ (“loan”), from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ- (“to leave”). Cognate of Danish leie. Doublet of lån and län.
From Old Swedish leghia, from Old Norse leiga, from Proto-Germanic *laigijaną (“to lend”).

parole.significato: (child's) play; typically denotes pleasurable and less rule-bound games and activities – "play" more in the sense of "e…
parole.testo: From Old Norse leikr.
From Old Swedish lēka, from Old Norse leika, from Proto-Germanic *laikaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

From Old Swedish līkami, līkamber, from Old Norse líkami, líkamr, from Proto-Germanic *līkahamô. Cognate with Icelandic líkami, Danish legeme, Dutch lichaam, German Leichnam. The final -n originally comes from the definite article.

parole.significato: a limb (major appendage of a human or animal)
parole.testo: From Old Norse limr, from Proto-Germanic *limuz (“branch, limb”) (compare English limb).
From Old Norse linr, from Proto-Germanic *linwaz.
From Old Swedish ler, from Old Norse leir. Cognate with Old Norse leira, Icelandic leir, Danish ler and Norwegian Bokmål leire.

parole.significato: search; look throughout (a place) for something
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lēta, from Old Norse leita, from Proto-Germanic *wlaitōną.
From Old Swedish lever, from Old Norse hleifr, from Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz. Cognate with Icelandic hleifur, English loaf, German Laib.
From Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją. Doublet of lövja (“medicine”).

parole.significato: to live, to be alive (concretely or figuratively)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish liva, from Old Norse lifa, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”). Cognate with Norwegian leve, Danish leve, Icelandic lifa, Dutch leven, German leben and English live.
From Old Swedish lēva, from Old Norse leifa, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”). Cognate with Icelandic leifa, English leave.
From Old Norse lifr, from Proto-Germanic *librō, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smudge, stick”), from *ley- (“to be slimy, be sticky, glide”).
leva + -nad. From Old Swedish lifnaþer, from Old Norse lifnaðr. Compare Danish levned.
Inherited from Old Swedish liþ, from Old Norse hlíð, from Proto-Germanic *hlīdō. Cognate of Latin clīvus, Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma), Old English hliþ.
From Old Swedish līþa, from Old Norse líða, from Proto-Germanic *līþaną.

parole.significato: a scythe (instrument for mowing grass, grain, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish līe, lē, from Old Norse lé, from Proto-Germanic *lewô, from Proto-Indo-European *leu- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: to lie; be in a horizontal position
parole.testo: From Old Swedish liggia, from Old Norse liggja, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.

parole.significato: looking like, resembling (in appearance or other characteristics)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish līker, from Old Norse líkr, from Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, from *ga- + *-līkaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish lik, from Old Norse lík, from Proto-Germanic *līką, from Proto-Indo-European *leyg-.

parole.significato: to the same degree, as, equally
parole.testo: From Old Norse líka, from Proto-Germanic *līkāną, *galīkāną.
From Old Norse lím.
From Old Norse lín, from Proto-Germanic *līną. Cognate with English linen.

parole.significato: a wire, a rope, a line
parole.testo: From Old Norse lína, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“line, rope, flaxen cord, thread”), from *līną (“flax”). Hypothetised to be derived from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”), although it's impossible to reconstruct a common PIE protoform due to discrepancies with other European branches and absence o
Inherited from Old Swedish lind, from Old Norse lind, from Proto-Germanic *lindō.

parole.significato: broad white cloth (particularly ones used for swaddling)
parole.testo: Oblique form of linde, from Old Swedish linde, lindi, from Old Norse lindi (“belt; girdle; sash; wrap”), likely related to Proto-Germanic *linþaz.

parole.significato: to carefully twist, bend, etc., (something) to accomplish something, with fiddly connotations; to coax
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish *liþka (compare Icelandic liðka), derived from Old Norse liðr (“member”). For the shift from -dk- to -rk- compare with burk. Doublet of led.
From Old Swedish list, from Old Norse list, from Proto-Germanic *listiz, from Proto-Indo-European *leys-, *leyǝs-. Cognate with Icelandic list.
From Old Norse hlíta, from a fusion of Proto-Germanic *wlītaną (“to see”) and a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”).
From Old Norse lítinn, accusative of lítill, from Proto-Germanic *lītilaz.
From Old Swedish līf, from Old Norse líf, from Proto-Germanic *lībą.
From liv (“life”) + -lig (“-ly”); from Old Norse lífligr.
From Old Swedish liuþ, from Old Norse hljóð, from Proto-Germanic *hleuþą. Cognate with Faroese ljóð, Norwegian lyd and ljod, Danish lyd, Icelandic hljóð, German Laut, Scots luid, Dutch luid.
From Old Swedish liūdha, from Old Norse hljóða (“sound”), equivalent to ljud + -a.

parole.significato: to lie, to tell an untruth
parole.testo: From Old Swedish liūgha, from Old Norse ljúga, from Proto-Germanic *leuganą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to tell a lie”). Cognate with Danish lyve, Faroese ljúgva (whence lúgva), Icelandic ljúga, Norwegian Bokmål lyve and Norwegian Nynorsk ljuga.
From Old Swedish liūs, from Old Norse ljóss, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-so-, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-.
From Old Swedish liūs, from Old Norse ljós, from Proto-Germanic *leuhsą, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-so-m, from Proto-Indo-European *lewk-.

From Old Swedish liuver, from Old Norse ljúfr, from Proto-Norse ᛚᛖᚢᛒᚨᛉ (leubaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *leubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *leubh- (“love”), *lewbʰ-. Related to English love, Latin libet, Russian любовь (ljubovʹ).
By surface analysis, ljuv + -lig. Diachronically, from Old Norse ljúfligr, from Proto-Germanic *leubalīkaz.
Inherited from Old Swedish lō, from Old Norse lóa, derived from or related to Proto-Germanic *luhsaz.

parole.significato: a lock of hair, a curl of hair
parole.testo: From Old Norse lok, lokkr, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz.

parole.significato: to attract, to lure, to entice
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lokka, lukka (“to kindly persuade”), from Old Norse lokka (“to lure, entice”), from Proto-Germanic *lukkōną (“to allure”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewgʰ- (“to lie”). Cognate with Icelandic lokka, Danish lokke.
Formed from a noun meaning "hair," (compare luden (“hairy”)) referring to the stripes on its flanks that look like hair, from or related to Old Norse loðinn (“shaggy, hairy”).

parole.significato: A barn with a strong and flat wooden floor, suitable for threshing or dancing.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish loe, from Old Norse lófi (“threshing floor”).
From Old Norse lomr, ultimately of imitative origin.
From Old Norse hlummr; along with Faroese lummur, both are probably ultimately from the same root as English loom (“apparatus for making fabric”).
From Old Swedish losna, from Old Norse losna. Equivalent to lös + -na. Doublet of lossa. Cognate of Danish løsne, Norwegian Bokmål løsne, Norwegian Nynorsk losna.

parole.significato: a part, a share, a piece, a portion (of a heritage, a lottery, of land, of fate)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish luter, loter, from Old Norse hlutr, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą, from Proto-Indo-European *klew-.
From Old Swedish luta, lota, from Old Norse hluta, from Proto-Germanic *hlutōną.
From Old Swedish lof, from Old Norse lof, from Proto-Germanic *lubą.
From Old Swedish lova, from Old Norse lofa, from Proto-Germanic *lubōną, equivalent to lov + -a. Cognate with Danish love, Norwegian love, Dutch loven, German loben.

parole.significato: a gap, a hole, an open slot, a small empty room
parole.testo: From Old Swedish loka, luka, from Old Norse lúka, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną, from Proto-Indo-European *lewg-. Compare English lock.
From Old Norse loðinn, from Proto-Germanic *ludanaz, past participle of *leudaną (“to sprout, to grow”).

parole.significato: calm, tranquil (of a person, weather, mood, situation, etc.)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lugn or lygn (“calm lake surface”), from Old Norse lygn. Compare Norwegian logn (“calm (without wind)”), and Icelandic lón (“calm water”).

parole.significato: smell, odor, scent (any smell, whether fragrant or offensive; scent; perfume)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lukt, from Middle Low German lucht, from Proto-Germanic *luftuz. Doublet of luft (“air”).

parole.significato: a grove, a lush wood with demanding flora
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lunder, from Old Norse lundr ("grove", "tree"), of unknown origin. Maybe akin to land or linda ("tree-field"). Masculine in Late Modern Swedish.

parole.significato: lung (organ that extracts oxygen from the air)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lunga, from Proto-Germanic *lungw- (literally “the light organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Compare Danish and Norwegian lunge, Icelandic lunga, German Lunge, lung.

From lunga (“lung”) + sot (“disease, sickness”). It should be noted that sot here is an archaic word for disease or sickness, inherited from Old Norse sótt, from Proto-Germanic *suhtiz. It is thus not related to the meaning of soot, which instead comes from Old Norse sót, from Proto-Germanic *sōtą.

parole.significato: a simple, straight horn (used as an instrument or for signaling)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lūdher (“horn, trumpet”), from Old Norse lúðr, from Proto-Germanic *lawwō, from Proto-Indo-European *lowH-éh₂.
From Old Swedish lūs, from Old Norse lús, from Proto-Germanic *lūs, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *luHs-, *lewH-.
From Old Norse losti (late Old Norse lyst), from Middle Low German lust lüst, lyst, from Old Saxon lust, from Proto-West Germanic *lustu.
From Old Swedish lusta, from Old Norse *lusta, from Proto-Germanic *lustōną.
From Old Swedish lūta, from Old Norse lúta, from Proto-Germanic *lūtaną.
From Old Norse hlý (“warmth”).

parole.significato: to close (a door, gate, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Norse lykja (preterit lukta), from Proto-Germanic *lukjaną (“to close, shut”).
From Old Swedish lyþa, from Old Norse hlýða, from Proto-Germanic *hliuþijaną.

parole.significato: to sound, to be worded, to have a wording
parole.testo: From Old Norse hljóða, probably via Danish lyde. Doublet of ljuda.

parole.significato: to lift; to move something upwards
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lypta, from Old Norse lypta, Proto-Germanic *luftijaną.
From Old Swedish lykt, a deverbal from lūka (“to close, to shut”), from Old Norse lúka, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną.
From Old Swedish lȳsa, from Old Norse lýsa. Compare dialectal ljusa, Norwegian lyse.
Present of obsolete lysta, from Old Norse lysta, Proto-Germanic *lustijaną. Related to lust.

parole.significato: lee (the state of not being windy due to something blocking the wind), (as a more common translation) shelter
parole.testo: From Old Norse hlé, from Proto-Germanic *hlewą.

parole.significato: a leak; a crack, crevice, fissure, or hole which admits water or other fluid, or lets it escape.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish læka, from Old Norse leka, from Proto-Germanic *lekaną.

parole.significato: leather (material produced by tanning animal skin)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lædher (“leather”), from Old Norse leðr (“leather”), from Proto-Germanic *leþrą.

From Old Norse legr, from Proto-Germanic *legrą, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to be situated, lie”). Related to ligga (“to lie”), lägga (“to lay”) and läge (“position”). Doublet of lager (“store”), derived through German Lager.
From Old Swedish lægger, from Old Norse leggr, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(ǝ)lak-, *lēk-.

parole.significato: to place lying (to lay) somewhere, to place/put in a lying position (not in a standing position); in particular used li…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish læggia, from Old Norse leggja, from Proto-Germanic *lagjaną. Causative of *ligjaną (see ligga).
From Old Norse lækna, from Proto-Germanic *lēkinōną. Cognate with Icelandic lækna.

From late Old Swedish lǣkiare, remade (by way of the agent suffix -are) from earlier Old Swedish lǣkir, from (east) Old Norse *lækir (cf. Old West Norse læknir), from Proto-Germanic *lēkijaz. Equivalent to läka (“heal”) + -are (“-er”). Identical in formation to Norwegian Nynorsk lækjar and Proto-Sla

parole.significato: to leave; to not take away with oneself but leave as available for others; to deposit
parole.testo: From earlier lemna, from Old Swedish limna, lifna, from Old Norse lifna, inchoative of Proto-Germanic *lībaną (“to remain, to be left”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp-.
From Old Norse lengd, from Proto-Germanic *langiþō.

parole.significato: a long time, during a long time, long
parole.testo: From Old Norse lengi.

parole.significato: a link (in a chain or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lænker, from Old Norse *hlenkr (cf. Old West Norse hlekkr), from Proto-Germanic *hlankiz.
From late Old Norse læra, lǽra, from Old Saxon lērian.
From Old Swedish lærikia, from Old Norse lævirki, from Proto-Germanic *laiwazikǭ.
From Old Swedish læsa, from Old Norse lesa, from Proto-Germanic *lesaną, from Proto-Indo-European *les-.
From Old Norse leistr, from Proto-Germanic *laistiz, from Proto-Indo-European *leys- (“track, furrow”). Cognate with English last.
From Old Swedish læte, from Old Norse læti. Cognate with Norwegian læte.
From Old Swedish lǣtter, from Old Norse léttr, from Proto-Germanic *linhtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁lengʷʰ-.
From late Old Swedish lætia, from earlier læti, from Old Norse leti. Cognate with Icelandic leti, Faroese leti, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐍄𐌴𐌹 (latei) and Old High German lazzī. Related with lat (“lazy”).

parole.significato: low, short; having a small height
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lāgher, from Old Norse lágr, from Proto-Germanic *lēgaz, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to lie”).

parole.significato: a flame (burning), a blaze, a flare
parole.testo: From Old Swedish loghi, lughi, from Old Norse logi, from Proto-Germanic *lugô. Related to Icelandic logi, Middle High German lohe, more distantly to Latin lucere (“to shine, to light”), Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “white”). All ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European *lewk-.
From Old Swedish lan, from Old Norse lán, from Proto-Germanic *laihną, from Proto-Indo-European *leykʷ-.
From Old Swedish lana, from Old Norse lána.
From Old Swedish langer, from Old Norse langr, from Proto-Germanic *langaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos. Compare English long, Dutch lang, German lang.
From Old Norse langskip. By surface analysis, lång (“long”) + skepp (“ship”).
From Old Swedish lar, from Old Norse lær, from Proto-Germanic *lahwaz.
From Old Norse lárr. Cognate of Finnish laari and Russian ларь (larʹ).
From Old Norse láss, from Proto-Germanic *lamsaz.
From Old Swedish læsa, from Old Norse læsa.

From Old Swedish lāta, from Old Norse láta, from Proto-Germanic *lētaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₁d- (“to let (go), be tired”). The sense “to sound” was also present in Old Norse and can be derived from the sense “to let (sound) go”.
Formed from låts, present tense of låtas, itself inherited from Old Norse látast.
From Old Norse lauðr, from Proto-Germanic *lauþrą, from Proto-Indo-European *lówh₃trom (“that which is used for washing”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash, bathe”).
From Old Swedish lø̄gh, from Old Norse laug, from Proto-Germanic *laugō.
From Old Swedish lœgha, from Old Norse lauga, from Proto-Germanic *laugō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃-. Cognate of Icelandic lauga.

From Old Swedish lyghn, possibly from Old Norse ljúga (“to lie”), but probably instead a loanword from Old Saxon lugina; both are ultimately from Proto-Germanic *luginō, itself from *leuganą (“to lie”).

parole.significato: contemptuous glee (at something or someone considered ridiculous), ridicule
parole.testo: Old Swedish löghe, from Old Norse hlœgi (“ridicule”), from Proto-Germanic *hlōgijaną (“to make laugh”), from Proto-Germanic *hlahjaną (“to laugh”). Compare Danish løjer, Icelandic hlægja.
From Old Swedish løgheliker, løghliker, from Old Norse hlœgiligr, hlœgligr. Equivalent to löje + -lig. Cognate with Icelandic hlægilegur, Norwegian Nynorsk løyeleg and Danish løjerlig.

parole.significato: onion (a genus of plants – see also Allium)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lø̄ker, from Old Norse laukr, from Proto-Norse ᛚᚨᚢᚲᚨᛉ (laukaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *laukaz.

parole.significato: reward, something given to someone for a deed or achievement
parole.testo: From Old Swedish løn, from Old Norse laun, from Proto-Germanic *launą, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w-.
From Old Swedish løna, from Old Norse launa, from laun + -a, equivalent to lön + -a. Cognate with Icelandic launa.
From Old Norse hlynr. Cognate with Danish løn, Norwegian lønn, Faroese lynur, Icelandic hlynur.
From Old Norse laun (“secrecy, concealment”), from Proto-Germanic *laugnaz (“hidden”).
From Old Norse laun (“secrecy, concealment”), from Proto-Germanic *laugnaz (“hidden”).

parole.significato: only used in i lönndom (“in secret”)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish løndom, cf. Danish løndom. Originally a dative plural form of lønd (“secret”) (cf. lagom and stundom), from Old Norse leynd (“secret”). Ultimately from the same root as ljuga (“to lie”). The pronunciation has undergone analogy with words ending in -dom (“-dom”), changing the pitch a
From Old Swedish lø̄pa, from Old Norse hlaupa, from Proto-Germanic *hlaupaną, from Proto-Indo-European *klewb- (“to spring, stumble”).

parole.significato: Saturday (now generally considered the sixth day of the week in non-religious contexts in Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish løghardagher, from Old Norse laugardagr.

parole.significato: loose; not tightened, able to move
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lø̄s, from Old Norse lauss, from Proto-Germanic *lausaz, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₁-.
From Old Swedish lø̄sa, from Old Norse leysa, from Proto-Germanic *lausijaną.
From Old Swedish lø̄sn, from Old Norse lausn from Proto-Germanic *lausīniz. Cognate of Danish løsen and Icelandic lausn.

parole.significato: a leaf (on a tree or bush and not a needle)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish løf, from Old Norse lauf, from Proto-Germanic *laubą, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *lewp- (“peel, break off”).

parole.significato: A remedy or potion; a medicine.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish lifia, lūfia, from Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją. Doublet of lev (“spell; potion”).
From Old Norse maðra, from Proto-Germanic *madarǭ.
From Old Swedish maghi, from Old Norse magi, from Proto-Germanic *magô, from Proto-Indo-European *mak-, *maks-.
From Old Swedish magher, from Old Norse magr (“thin, meager”), from Proto-Germanic *magraz, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.

parole.significato: a state of leisure; almost exclusively used in the expression
parole.testo: From Old Swedish mak, assumed to originate from an unattested Old Swedish adjective *maker (“easy, calm, fit, suiting, appropriate”), from Old Norse makr (“easy to deal with”). From Old Swedish maka, oblique form of maki, from Old Norse maki, from Proto-Germanic *makô. Doublet of make. Because of the -a usually interpreted as feminine.

From Old Swedish munder, from Old Norse muðr, munnr, from Proto-Germanic *munþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ment-.

From Old Swedish mynta, from Old Norse minta, from Middle Low German minte, münte, from Old Saxon minta, from Proto-West Germanic *mintā, from Latin menta.

parole.significato: to measure (determine a measurement with respect to some unit)
