parole.significato: a pinch, a dash; a small amount of powder or granules
parole.testo: From Old Swedish niūpa, from Old Norse *hnjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *hneupaną (“to pluck”). Related to Gothic 𐌳𐌹𐍃𐌷𐌽𐌹𐌿𐍀𐌰𐌽 (dishniupan, “to break apart”).

From Old Swedish hiupon (possibly nominative plural), from Old Norse *hjúpa, from Proto-Germanic *heupǭ. Compare Danish hyben, Norwegian nype, hjupa, Old Saxon hiopo, Old High German hiufo, dialectal German hiefen, hüfen, Old English héope and English hip. The initial n- is the product of metanalysi
From Old Swedish niūsa, from Old Norse hnjósa, from Proto-Germanic *hneusaną.

parole.significato: a clew (a ball of yarn or string), a skein
parole.testo: The noun ending -n was added in the 16th or 17th century. The older noun is the same as the verb, nysta (“to clew, roll yarn/thread into a ball”), from an Old Norse *hniusta. The root appears to exist in Old Norse nista, nesta, Danish næste (“to tack, to sew together”), in older related words knu-/h
From Old Norse nebbi, from Proto-Germanic *nabją. Further origin unknown.

parole.significato: A Näcken, a nix (noun contra proper noun); a male water-spirit in human form, mainly residing in rivers and lakes, who…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish neker, näkker, from Old Norse nykr, from Proto-Germanic *nikwiz-, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“wash”, verb). First attested in 1430. Cognate with Old English nicor, Danish nøk, nøkke, Old Danish jucker, Norwegian nykk, Icelandic nykr, and Dutch nik

From Old Swedish *nædher, *næþer, from Old Norse naðr (“adder, snake in general”), from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ (“adder, snake in general”). Cognate to Icelandic naður (“adder”). Compare English adder (“viper”) vs deaf adder (“slowworm”).

Feminine form of näder. From Old Norse naðra, feminine form of naðr (“adder, snake in general”), from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ (“adder, snake in general”). Cogngate to Icelandic naðra, feminine form of naður (“adder”). Compare English adder (“viper”) vs deaf adder (“slowworm”).
From Old Swedish næmna, from Old Norse nefna, nemna, from Proto-Germanic *namnijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

parole.significato: to have the heart or conscience to do something unpleasant or hurtful.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nænnas, nænna, from Old Norse nenna, from Proto-Germanic *nanþijaną. Cognate to Danish nænne and Icelandic nenna.
From Old Norse nær, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz, comparative of *nēhw. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).

Derived from Old Swedish när (“near”, adverb), from Old Norse nær (“nearer”, comparative adverb), from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz, comparative of *nēhw. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”). The comparative närmare and superlative närmast are from närmare and närmaster respectively,
From Old Norse næstr, a superlative of ná (“near”), corresponding to Proto-Germanic *nēhwist (“nearest, closest”).

parole.significato: to stitch (together), to sew (quickly and loosely)
parole.testo: From Old Norse nesta, nista (“to pin, nail fast”), from Proto-Germanic *nestjaną, likely related to *natją (“net”).

parole.significato: net; a mesh of string, cord, or rope.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish næt, from Old Norse net, from Proto-Germanic *natją, from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to turn, twist, knot”).

parole.significato: a fist (referring to a hand more generally, not necessarily clenched)
parole.testo: From Old Norse hnefi, compare with Norwegian Bokmål neve.
From Old Swedish na, from Old Norse ná. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach, to attain”).
From Old Norse náð. Cognate with Danish, Norwegian Bokmål nåde, Icelandic náð, and German Gnade.

From late Old Swedish naghan, from earlier nokon, accusative of Old Swedish nokor, from Old Norse nǫkkurr, from Proto-Norse *ne-wait-ek-hwarjaʀ (literally, "not-know-I-who"). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk nokon, Danish nogen, Faroese nakar, Icelandic nokkur, Norwegian Bokmål noen.

parole.significato: any, some, anything, something (neuter form of någon)
parole.testo: From Old Norse nǫkkurr, contracted from ne veit ek hverr (“I don't know which one”). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk nokon.

parole.significato: a needle, a pin (implement for sewing, crocheting, attaching stuff, etc.; however not for knitting)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nāl, from Old Norse nál, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō.
From Old Norse nauð, from Proto-Norse *ᚾᚨᚢᛞᛁᛉ (*naudiʀ), from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, *nauþiz. Cognate with English need, German Not.

parole.significato: to have to, to be forced to (do something, due to circumstances)
parole.testo: From nödga, from Old Swedish nöþgha, from Old Norse nauðga.
From Old Swedish nø̄ghia, from Old Norse nœgja.
From Old Swedish nut, not, from Old Norse hnot, from Proto-Germanic *hnuts. The irregular stem vowel change in modern Swedish was due to influence from the plural form.

parole.significato: cattle, especially in compounds such as nötkreatur (“cattlebeast”, cf. English neatbeast), or nötkött (“beef”)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish nø̄t, from Old Norse naut, from Proto-Germanic *nautą, from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to acquire, make use of”).

parole.significato: Added to adjectives to yield their opposites; un-
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ō-, from Old Norse ú-, ó-, from Proto-Germanic *un-, from the Proto-Indo-European *n̥- whence also Greek α- (a-) and English un-.

parole.significato: and; used to connect two homogeneous (similar) words or phrases
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ock, ok, from Old Norse ok, unstressed variant of Proto-Germanic *auk (“also”). Cognate with Norwegian, Danish and Icelandic og, Dutch ook, German auch, and English eke. The unusual spelling with the digraph ch may have been to avoid confusion with the now dated ock (“too, also”).
From Old Swedish ok, from Old Norse auk.
From Old Swedish oker, uker, from Old Norse ókr, okr, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz. Cognate of Norwegian åger, Danish åger, German Wucher, Dutch woeker, English oker, Gothic 𐍅𐍉𐌺𐍂𐍃 (wōkrs).
Corresponding to och / ock + så, from Old Swedish ok svā, from Old Norse ok and svá. Compare Danish også.

parole.significato: of inherited (land) property rights (of the noun); allodial, especially from time immemorial
parole.testo: From Old Swedish oþol, oþal, odhel, from Old Norse óðal, from Proto-Germanic *ōþalą. Cognate with Danish and Norwegian Bokmål odel, Norwegian Nynorsk odal, Faroese and Icelandic óðal. Compare odel (“soil”), odling (“cultivation”), odla (“to cultivate”).

parole.significato: bog bilberry, Vaccinium uliginosum (berry and shrub)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish oþer (“raging, wild”), from Old Norse óðr, suffixed with -on (appearing in the names of many berries and some fruits). Perhaps in reference to supposed toxicity.
From Old Norse offr.
From Old Norse oft, from Proto-Germanic *ufta.
From Old Norse ok, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm. Doublet of zygot.
From Old Swedish okunnogher, from Old Norse úkunnigr, from Proto-Germanic *unkunþīgaz, equivalent to o- + kunnig.
From Old Norse úlíkr, from Proto-Germanic *ungalīkaz. By surface analysis, o- + lik. Compare English unlike, Dutch ongelijk, Faroese ólíkur, German ungleich, Norwegian Bokmål ulik.

parole.significato: The letter "O" in the Swedish spelling alphabet
parole.testo: From Old Swedish Olāver, Olēf, from Old Norse Óláfr, from Proto-Norse *ᚨᚾᚢᛚᚨᛁᛒᚨᛉ (*anulaibaʀ). First recorded as a given name in Sweden in 1400. Cognate with Norwegian Olav and English Olaf.

From Old Norse um, from Proto-Germanic *umbi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰi. * As a conjunction, um superseded or blended with Old Norse ef and em, taking on their function as well. This is from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”), whence also English if and German ob. Doublet of jäv, direct desc

parole.significato: a proxy, a representative, a delegate
parole.testo: From Old Swedish umbuþ‚ from Old Norse umboð. Akin to om + bud.

From Old Swedish umbuds man or ombud (“representative, proxy”) + man. The origin of the word is found in Old Norse umboðsmaðr and the word “umbuds man”, meaning representative. The first preserved use in Swedish is from 1552.

parole.significato: a round (stage of some greater whole)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish umganger, from Old Norse umgangr, from Proto-Germanic *umbigangaz, equivalent to om + gång.
From Old Norse umkring, equivalent to om + kring (“around”).
From Old Swedish ōnder, vānder, from Old Norse vándr. Compare Swedish vånda, våda, Old English onda.

parole.significato: Wednesday (now generally considered the third day of the week in non-religious contexts in Sweden)
parole.testo: The word is originally a short form for Odens dag, meaning day of Oden. (Note: "Oden" and "Odin" are alternative spellings of the same name.) From Old Swedish oþinsdagher, from Old Norse óðinsdagr (“Odin's day”), from Proto-West Germanic *Wōdanas dag.
From Old Swedish orþ, from Old Norse orð, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”).

parole.significato: the strength or power to do something
parole.testo: Deverbative of orka (“to have strength”), from Old Norse orka, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”).

parole.significato: to have strength, will, or stamina enough
parole.testo: From Old Swedish orka, from Old Norse orka, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (English work), from Proto-Indo-European *wṛǵ-·.

parole.significato: serpent, snake, or therof slithering legless animal (cf. kopparorm, “slowworm”, sandorm, “sandworm” in the book series…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ormber (“snake/dragon, worm/vermin, ringworm”), from Old Norse ormr, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis, *wrmo- (“serpent, scorpion, maggot, worm”), maybe from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to turn = slither?”). Akin to English worm, wyrm. Doublet of vurm.
From Old Norse *runa, from runi (“boar”).
From Old Norse orri. Cognate with Faroese orri, Elfdalian uorre.
From Old Norse óréttr, from Proto-Germanic *unrehtaz. By surface analysis, o- + rätt.

parole.significato: a river mouth; the place where a creek, stream or river enters into a lake
parole.testo: From Old Norse óss.
From Old Norse oss, from Proto-Germanic *uns, from Proto-Indo-European *n̥smé.
From Old Swedish oster, from Old Norse ostr, from Proto-Germanic *justaz, from Proto-Indo-European *yéwHs.
otal + -ig, from Old Swedish otalliker, from Old Norse útalligr. Compare with Danish utallig, Norwegian utallig, and German unzählig.
From Old Swedish ōtta, ōta, from Old Norse ótta.
o- (“un-”) + täck (“pretty; beautiful”). From Old Swedish othäkker, from Old Norse þekkr (“pleasing”). Cognate with Icelandic óþekkur (“naughty, rude”).
Inherited from Old Swedish ovan, from Old Norse ofan, from Proto-Germanic *ubanē. Cognate with Danish oven and German oben, as well as with the compound forms Dutch boven and English above.

parole.significato: bad weather, usually with heavy precipitation and strong winds; a storm; bad weather
parole.testo: From Old Norse úveðr, óveðr, from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą. Equivalent to o- + väder. Compare English unweather.

parole.significato: an ox (adult castrated male of cattle, typically used as a beast of burden)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish oxe, from Old Norse oxi, uxi, from Proto-Germanic *uhsô, from Proto-Indo-European *uksḗn (“bull”).

parole.significato: a toad (an amphibian similar to a frog with bigger back legs and more ragged skin)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish padda, from Old Norse padda. Of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bed- (“to swell”) (Pok. 96), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell”) (Pok. 98-102), which would indicate a Proto-Germanic *paddǭ. Cognate with Icelandic padda, Danish padde. Compare English

parole.significato: a stool ((small) chair without armrests or back)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish pall (“bench, footstool”), from Old Norse pallr (“bench, platform, stage”), from Middle Low German palle (“ship's deck”). Sense of "cargo pallet" perhaps influenced by English pallet.
From Old Swedish palmber, palma, from Old Norse palmi, from Latin palma.
From Old Norse panna, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ.
From Old Swedish papir, from late Old Norse pappir, from Middle Low German papīr, pappīr, from Old French papier.
From Old Norse paradís, from Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos), ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah.
From Old Swedish parker, from a Old Norse *parkʀ, from Proto-Norse *ᛈᚨᚱᚨᚲᚨᛉ (*parakaʀ), from a Proto-Germanic *parrukaz; ultimately assumed to stem from French.
From Old Norse peningr and pengr. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *panningaz.
From Old Norse penningr, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Cognate with English penny.
From Old Swedish pepar, pipar, from Old Norse piparr, from Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi). Cognate with Danish peber, Norwegian pepper, pepar.

parole.significato: The letter "P" in the Swedish spelling alphabet
parole.testo: From Old Norse Pétr, from Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος (Pétros), from πέτρος (pétros, “stone, rock”), related to πέτρα (pétra). Later reinforced by the German Peter.

parole.significato: to peck, to pick (of a bird, or with a pointed instrument)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish pikka, from Old Norse, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną. Compare English pick.

parole.significato: a maid, a female servant; female employee on a farm, as in a milkmaid.
parole.testo: From Old Norse píka. Cognate with Icelandic píka and Danish pige. Also cognate with Finnish piika, Estonian piiga, and arguably, with Chuvash пике́ (pik̬é, “noblewoman, beauty”). Difficult to determine which language borrowed from which.
From Old Swedish pigger, perhaps from Old Norse píkr (“nail, spike”). Cognate with Danish pig. Related also to Swedish pik and Old Norse pík.
Inherited from Old Swedish pīker, from Old Norse pík, from Proto-Germanic *pīkaz.
From Old Norse píla.
From Old Norse píli.
From Old Swedish pilagrimber, from Old Norse pílagrímr, from Medieval Latin pelegrinus, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner, traveler”).
From Old Norse piltr. Cognate with Icelandic piltur and Norwegian pilt, Danish pilt.

Inherited from Old Swedish pina, from Old Norse pína, from Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ). Cognate of Danish pine, Icelandic pína, German Pein. Compare origin of English pain, French peine.

parole.significato: a stick (elongated piece of wood (or other material), like a (severed) branch, or processed)
parole.testo: From Old Norse pinni, from Middle Low German pinne, from Old Saxon pinn (“pin; peg”), from Proto-Germanic *pinn- (“pointed object; spike; peak”), from Proto-Indo-European *bend- (“protruding object, pointed peg, nail, edge”). Cognate with English pin.
From Old Norse *pípa.
From Old Norse pípa. Doublet of pip.
From Old Norse plagg, from Proto-Germanic *plaggą.

parole.significato: place; any geographical position a little larger than just a point, such as a village, city or just a "nowhere"
parole.testo: From Old Swedish platz, from Old Norse plaz, from Middle Low German plātze, from Old French place, from Latin platea.
From Old Swedish plokka, plukka, from Old Norse, from Proto-Germanic *plukkōną. Compare English pluck.
From Old Norse plógr, from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz, *plōguz.
From Old Norse plástr, borrowed from Middle Low German plaster, plāster, from Old Saxon plāstar, from Proto-West Germanic *plastr.

parole.significato: to plow, to plough (soil, or with similar sense extensions to English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish plø̄ghia, from Old Norse plœgja, from Proto-Germanic *plōgijaną.
From late Old Norse port n, portr m, from Latin porta f. Computing sense a semantic loan from English.
From Old Norse pottr (“pot, tub, basin”), from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”). Doublet of potta.
From Old Swedish pris, from Late Old Norse príss, from Middle Low German pris, from Old French pris, from Latin pretium.
From Old Norse prófeti, prófeta, from Late Latin propheta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs).
From Old Swedish prydha, from Old Norse prýða, probably a borrowing from Old English prūd (“proud, noble”). Compare Danish pryde.
From Old Swedish præster, from Old Norse prestr.
From Old Norse prámr, from Middle Low German prām, from Old Czech *prám, from Proto-Slavic *pormъ.

From Old Swedish salmber, psalmber, from Old Norse salmr, psalmr, from Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós, “the sound emenating from twitching or twanging perhaps with the hands or fingers, mostly of musical strings”).
From Old Swedish pund, from Old Norse pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą, from Latin pondo.

parole.significato: a pouch, a purse (small bag that can be closed with drawstring or the like, used to keep small items)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish punger, from Old Norse pungr, itself of unknown origin.

parole.significato: to pant, to puff (as after exertion)
parole.testo: From or related to Old Norse pustr (“slap in the face”), according to Pokorny, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to swell, inflate”). Cognate of Danish puste, German pusten. Doublet of pussig, pysa, and pösa. See also origin of kindpust.

parole.significato: to lightly push (apply force to an object to as to make it move)
parole.testo: From Old Norse pota, from Proto-Germanic *putōną.

parole.significato: to (cause to) stream out (with a hissing sound) (of some gas, for example air from a balloon)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish pysa, from Old Norse *pýsa, from Proto-Germanic *pusjaną, from *pus- (“swelling, bladder”), ultimately from the same root as pusta (“to puff”).
From Old Norse pilz, from Middle Low German pels, from Medieval Latin pellicea, from Latin pellis (“skin”). Cognate with Icelandic pels.

parole.significato: on, on top of; touching from above
parole.testo: Rebracketing of uppå, from Old Norse upp á. Compare English 'pon, formed in a similar way from upon.
From Old Swedish pāfughl, from Old Norse páfugl.

parole.significato: a bag (soft container open at the top, usually made of paper, plastic, or fabric)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish posi, from Old Norse posi, from Proto-Germanic *pusô.

From Old Norse páskar, from Medieval Latin pascha, from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), from Aramaic פסחא (pasḥa), from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pesaḥ). Compare Danish påske, Norwegian Bokmål påske, Norwegian Nynorsk påske.
From Old Swedish pave, pavi, from Old Norse páfi, from Old Saxon pavos (perhaps via Middle Low German pawes), from Old French pape, from Latin papa.

parole.significato: a puddle, a pool of water
parole.testo: From Old Norse pœla, pollr, from Proto-Germanic *pōlaz.

parole.significato: a mongrel (dog of mixed or uncertain origin)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rakke (“dog”), from Old Norse rakki (“dog”).

parole.significato: A person of dishonorable social status who performs (necessary) taboo jobs; such as assistant to an executioner; a knac…
parole.testo: From Old Norse rakki.

parole.significato: a row; a line of entries in a table, or a line of objects
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫð, from Proto-Germanic *radō (“row”).

parole.significato: coarse fur, bristles (hair of an animal, especially unordered, wild, rugged, shaggy hair)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫgg, from Proto-Germanic *rūhaz (“coarse, rough”). Same as Danish rag, Icelandic rogg, Norwegian ragg, Old English adjective raggig and English noun rag, Icelandic rýja (“to rip the wool from sheep, to shear”), Latin ruo (“to rip, dig”) and rutrum (“a shovel”). In older times, wool w
From Old Norse rakr, related to rekja (“to unwind; to trace”). Compare English right.

parole.significato: a front paw of a bear
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ramber, Old Norse hrammr (“bear's claw; paw”).
From Old Norse rǫnd, cognate with Icelandic rönd.

parole.significato: to carefully and critically examine, to scrutinize (often introspectively)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ransaka (“house-search”), from rann, corresponding to Icelandic rann (“house”), related to granne (“neighbor”), and a verb saka, derived from söka (“to search”); from Old Norse rannsaka.
From Old Norse hrapa, from Proto-Germanic *hrapaną, *hrappa- (“fast”), from Proto-Indo-European *krb(ʰ)- (“quickly”).

parole.significato: a race (a large group of individuals of the same species set apart from others on the basis of a common heritage), a br…
parole.testo: From Old Norse rás (“race”), from Proto-Germanic *rēsō.
From Old Norse rasa.

parole.significato: a break (rest or pause, usually from work)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rǫst, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, *rastijō (“rest”), from Proto-Indo-European *ros-, *res-, *erH- (“rest”).
From Old Norse hrata, from Proto-Germanic *hratt- (“to rush”); see *hradaz (“hasty, quick”). Cognate with Icelandic hrata (“to lose balance”) and Old English hratian (“to hurry”).
From Old Swedish rēþa, from Old Norse reiða.
From Old Swedish redh, from Old Norse reiðr, from Middle Low German rêde, reide, from Old Saxon *rēda, from Proto-Germanic *raidō (“ride, journey”). Doublet of red (“ride; raid”).
From Old Norse hreiðr.
From Old Swedish ræghn, from Old Norse regn, from Proto-Germanic *regną.
Old Norse regna, from Proto-Germanic *regnōną, verbal form of *regną (“rain”)
From Old Norse regnbogi (“rainbow”), from Proto-Germanic *regnabugô.
From Old Norse *regndropi, from Proto-Germanic *regnadrupô. Equivalent to regn + droppe.
From Old Swedish räghnogher, reghnogher, from Old Norse *regnugr, from Proto-Germanic *regnagaz (“rainy”), equivalent to regn + -ig.
From Old Norse reim.
Inherited from Old Norse hreinn n.
From Old Norse hreinn (“clean”), from Proto-Germanic *hrainiz.

parole.significato: to remove undesired things (from something); to clean (out), to clear (out), to purge, to wipe, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rēnsa, rænsa, from Old Norse hreinsa, from Proto-Germanic *hrainisōną.
From Old Norse reip, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *raipą, *raipaz, from Proto-Indo-European *roypnós (“strap, band, rope”).

parole.significato: to cause to become upright; to erect
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rēsa, from Old Norse reisa, from Proto-Germanic *raizijaną.
From Old Norse reita, from Proto-Germanic *wraitijaną.
From Old Norse reifa, from Proto-Germanic *raibōną. Compare Old English ārāfian (“uncoil; wind off”), Faroese reiva (“swaddle”).

parole.significato: a reef; rocks close to the water surface.
parole.testo: From Old Norse rif. Compare Danish rev, Middle Low German rif, German Riff.
From rev (“rib”) + ben (“bone”), from Old Swedish rif (+ bēn), from Old Norse rif, from Proto-Germanic *ribją. Doublet of ribba.
From Old Swedish ridh (“while, bout [of illness]”), from Old Norse hríð (“snowstorm”).

parole.significato: to ride (as on a horse or other mount – compare åka)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish riþa, from Old Norse ríða, from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną.
From Old Norse riddari, from Middle Low German ridder (“rider, knight”).

From Old Swedish rīker, from Old Norse ríkr, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz, a derivative of Proto-Germanic *rīks (“king, ruler”), itself a borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs.
From Old Norse ríki, from Proto-Germanic *rīkiją, from Proto-Germanic *rīks, an early borrowing from Proto-Celtic *rīxs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rḗǵs. Cognate with Dutch rijk and German Reich.

parole.significato: wealth, riches (of money, possessions, or more generally)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rīkedōmber, rīkdōmber, from Old Norse ríkdómr, from Proto-Germanic *rīkijadōmaz, equivalent to rik + -dom. Compare English richdom.
From Old Norse rím, from Proto-Germanic *rīmą.

parole.significato: ring; a circular piece of material
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ringer, from Old Norse hringr, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz.

parole.significato: to ring; to make a bell produce a sound
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ringia, ringa, from Old Norse hringja, from Proto-Germanic *hringijaną. Cognate with Danish ringe, Norwegian ringe or ringa, Old English hringan, English ring.
From Old Swedish rinna, from Old Norse rinna, from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną.
From Old Norse rjúpa.

parole.significato: small shrubs, such as blueberry and lingonberry; bush, scrub, undergrowth, brushwood
parole.testo: From Old Norse hrís.
From Old Norse rís, from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα (óruza). Akin to English rice.
Inherited from Old Norse hrista, from Proto-Germanic *hristijaną. Cognate of Icelandic hrista.

parole.significato: to draw (usually simpler, more line-based pictures or drawings – compare teckna)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish hrīta, from Old Norse hríta, from Proto-Germanic *hrītaną (“to draw, to scratch”).
From Old Swedish rīva, from Old Norse rífa, from Proto-Germanic *rīfaną.

parole.significato: to row; to transport oneself in a small boat, with help of oars
parole.testo: From Old Norse róa, from Proto-Germanic *rōaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁-.
From Old Norse *rukka, rugga, from Proto-Germanic *rukkōną.

From Old Swedish roliker (“calm, quiet”), from Old Norse róligr. Equivalent to ro + -lig. Cognate with Old Danish rowelig, rolic, Danish rolig (“calm, quiet”), Norwegian Bokmål rolig (“calm, quiet”), Norwegian Nynorsk roleg (“calm, quiet, steady”), Low German rauelik and German ruhig (“calm, quiet”)

From Old Swedish rughn, romn, from Old Norse hrogn, from Proto-Germanic *hrugnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“frogspawn”); cognate with Danish and Norwegian rogn, Icelandic hrogn, German Rogen, and English roe.

parole.significato: a cry, a call, a shout
parole.testo: From Old Norse hróp.
From Old Swedish rōpa, from Old Norse hrópa, from Proto-Germanic *hrōpaną. Cognate with Faroese rópa, Icelandic hrópa, Danish råbe, Norwegian rope.

From Old Swedish rosa, from Old Norse hrósa, from the same root as hróðr (“praise”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōþrą. Cognate with Danish rose. Compare German Ruhm (“glory”), Gothic 𐌷𐍂𐍉𐌸𐌴𐌹𐌲𐍃 (hrōþeigs, “glorious”). Related to berömma.

parole.significato: Any container meant for collection and temporary storage of garbage, such as wastepaper basket, garbage can, dustbin, b…
parole.testo: From Old Norse rosk (“litter, waste”).

Probably related to Norwegian røslig, Norwegian Nynorsk røseleg, rausleg (“big, powerful, burly”), analog to Old Norse hrøsniligr, from Old Norse rausn (“pride”), to the same root as Swedish rosa, Old Norse hrósa (“to praise, boast”). Potentially also related to rosande in the sense of “hotheaded, l
From Old Swedish rost, from Old Norse *rustr, from Proto-Germanic *rustaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-.

parole.significato: root; the part of a plant that anchors the plant body
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rōt, from Old Norse rót, from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds.
From Old Swedish rotfaster, from Old Norse rótfastr, equivalent to rot + fast. Compare rare English rootfast.

parole.significato: to move (something) slightly (often out of its ordinary or intended position); to nudge, to dislodge
parole.testo: Related to Icelandic rubba (“to scrape”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Old Norse riūfa, rjúfa (“to break open, clear away”). Likely cognate of English rub.

parole.significato: a deckhouse; a pilothouse; a cabin (room above or below deck on a boat)
parole.testo: First attested in 1730, from Old Norse hróf (“boat shed, shack”), although effected by Dutch roef and Low German ruf (compare Norwegian ruff). Originally of the roof of the deckhouse. Also found as dialectal Northern Gutnish roffe (“shack, old house”). Cognate with English roof.

parole.significato: a rune ((representation of a) letter of the runic alphabet)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rūna, rūn, from Old Norse rún, from Proto-Norse ᚱᚢᚾᛟ (runo, acc. sing.), from Proto-Germanic *rūnō.
From Old Swedish russ, from Old Norse hross, from Proto-Germanic *hrussą, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers-. Doublet of horse and kärra; related to karriär.
From Old Norse rúsína.
From Old Norse rotinn.

rutten + -a, Old Swedish rutna, rotna, same as Danish rådne, Norwegian Bokmål råtne, Icelandic rotna. The adjective rutten (“rotten”) originated as the past participle of a different verb than this one, one of strong conjugation. Both verbs ultimately relate to röta (“rot”). From Old Norse rotna.

parole.significato: to yank, to jerk, to pull quickly
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish rykka, rykkia, from Old Norse rykkja, from Proto-Germanic *rukkijaną. Doublet of rucka.

parole.significato: back; the rear of the body; especially the part between the neck and the end of the spine
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rygger, from Old Norse hryggr, from Proto-Germanic *hrugjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krewk.
From Old Swedish riūka, from Old Norse rjúka, from Proto-Germanic *reukaną. See also rök.

parole.significato: to hold (a certain volume of space)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rȳma, from Old Norse rýma, from Proto-Germanic *rūmijaną. Related to rum (“room”).

From Old Norse hrjósa, from Proto-Germanic *hreusaną (“to shudder, shiver, quiver”), from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“raw meat, fresh blood”). Related to Old Norse hrār (“raw, fresh, juicy”), Old English hrēaw, hrēow (“raw”), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬏𐬭𐬀 (xrūra, “bloody, gruesome, cruel”), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬥𐬙 (xruu
From Old Swedish riūta, rȳta, from Old Norse hrjóta, from Proto-Germanic *hreutaną.

parole.significato: to stretch out (some body part) in some direction (without handing something over or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rækkia, from Old Norse rekja, from Proto-Germanic *rakjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵéyeti.
From Old Norse hræðast, passive of Old Norse hræða.
From Old Swedish rǣdder, from the past participle of Old Swedish rǣþa (“to frighten”), from Old Norse hræða (past participle hræddr), from Proto-Germanic *hrēdijaną.
From Old Swedish rædsla, from Old Norse hræzla, equivalent to räda (“to scare”) + -sla. Cognate with Icelandic hræðsla.
Inherited from Old Swedish rækna, from Late Old Norse reikna, which is borrowed from Middle Low German rekenen. Cognate with Icelandic reikna, English reckon, Ukrainian рахувати (raxuvaty).
From Old Swedish räþelīker, from Old Norse hræðiligr. Cognate to Danish ræddelig and Icelandic hræðilegur.

From Old Norse rifna, equivalent to riva (“to tear, to demolish”) + -na (“inchoative suffix”). -mn- via the sound change -fn- > -mn-, compare namn (< Old Norse nafn) and somna, lämna, formed in the same manner.

parole.significato: a narrow, natural or constructed channel (usually open at the top) that conveys or might convey water (or another liqui…
parole.testo: Probably from Old Norse renna, yielding also Icelandic renna, Norwegian renne, Danish rende; from Proto-Germanic *rannijǭ, Also related to Gothic 𐍂𐌹𐌽𐌽𐍉 (rinnō), Old High German rinna (both from *rinnǭ).

parole.significato: to run ((back and forth) in a somewhat wild, hectic, or unruly manner – sometimes hyperbolically)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rænna, Old Norse renna, from Proto-Germanic *rannijaną. Originally causative of rinna.
From Old Swedish rǣtter, rǣter, from Old Norse réttr, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós. Doublet of rätt.
From Old Norse réttr, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós. Doublet of rät.
From Old Swedish rǣtta, from Old Norse rétta, from Proto-Germanic *rihtijaną. Akin to rätt + -a.

From Old Swedish rætfærdhogher, from Old Norse réttferðugr, from Middle Low German rechtverdich, from Old Saxon reht (“right”) + fard (“journey”) + -ig. The Middle Low German is also the source of German rechtfertigen, Danish retfærdig, Norwegian rettferdig.
From Old Norse refr, from Proto-Norse *rebaʀ, ultimately borrowed from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hrawpāćás (“fox, jackal”), through some intermediaries.
From Old Swedish rar, from Old Norse hrár, from Proto-Germanic *hrawaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂-.

parole.significato: a yard, a stick, a beam
parole.testo: From Old Norse rá (“sailyard, pole for drying fish”), from Proto-Germanic *rahō, cognate with Middle Low German rā, German Rah.
From Old Norse rá, from Proto-Germanic *raihô, *raihą, cognate to German Rah, Rahe.
From Old Norse rá (“landmark”).
From Old Norse ráð, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *Hréh₁dʰos, from *Hreh₁dʰ- (“to think, arrange”).
From Old Swedish rāþa, from Old Norse ráða, from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną.

parole.significato: To arrange, to fix, to fix up.
parole.testo: Potentially related to reda (“order, orderliness”), from Old Swedish rēþa, from Old Norse reiða.
From Old Swedish rogher, from Old Norse rugr, from Proto-Germanic *rugiz. Cognate with Danish rug, Icelandic rúgur, Dutch rogge, German Roggen, and English rye.
Inherited from Old Norse hrókr, from Proto-Germanic *hrōkaz (“crow, rook”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“to crow”); see rook for more.

parole.significato: a robbery (act or practice of robbing)
parole.testo: From Old Norse rán.
From Old Swedish rø̄þer, from Old Norse rauðr, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰós < *h₁rewdʰ-.
From Old Swedish rydhia, from Old Norse ryðja, from Proto-Germanic *rudjaną.

parole.significato: disclose; expose, reveal (secret information); to betray (a secret)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish røghia (“to accuse, blame; to bewray, rat out, disclose”), from Old Norse rǿgja, from Proto-Germanic *wrōgijaną. Related to Norwegian røyja, Icelandic rægja.
From Old Norse reykr, from Proto-Germanic *raukiz. Cognate to German Rauch. See also the related ryka.

parole.significato: to smoke (tobacco or the like, currently or as a habit)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish rø̄kia, from Old Norse reykja, from Proto-Germanic *raukijaną.

parole.significato: finding, observation (thing to come out of the (scientific) study of something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse raun. Cognate of Ancient Greek ἔρευνα (éreuna).
Inherited from Old Swedish rø̄na, from Old Norse reyna. By surface analysis, rön + -a. Cognate of Danish rønne, Icelandic reyna.
From Old Norse reynir (“rowan”), related to rauðr (“red”). Compare Norwegian rogn and Danish røn.
From Old Swedish rør, from Old Norse reyrr.
From Old Swedish rø̄ra, from Old Norse hrœra, from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną.
From the Old Norse hreysi (“a cairn; a pile of stones”). Related to Norwegian Nynorsk røys f (“cairn”).

parole.significato: voice (sound uttered by the mouth, especially that uttered by human beings in speech or song)
parole.testo: From Old Norse raust, ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to flow, boil, stream, move”). Related to Proto-Germanic *runsiz (“river”). Cognate with Danish røst.
From Old Norse rauf (“gap, rift, hole”), cognate with Danish røv.

parole.significato: to rob; to commit robbery or looting
parole.testo: From Old Swedish röva, from Old Norse reyfa, from Proto-Germanic *raubijaną, with influence from Middle Low German rôven. Equivalent to rov + -a.
From Old Norse sǫðull, from Proto-Germanic *sadulaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sod-tlō-, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“to sit”).

From Old Swedish sagha, from Old Norse saga, from Proto-Germanic *sagǭ. First attested in the mid-14th century Cognate with Danish saghæ, Jutish save (“a narrative, a narration, a tale, a report”), Norwegian Nynorsk soge, Faroese søga, Icelandic saga, German Sage, English saw. Perhaps related to Lit

parole.significato: a thing (concrete or abstract – also of events, like in English)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Norse sǫk, from Proto-Germanic *sakō. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål sak, Norwegian Nynorsk sak, Danish sag, Icelandic sök, English sake, Dutch zaak, German Low German Saak, Sook, German Sache. An unrelated word that also underwent the transformation in meaning from "legal matter" to
sak (“legal dispute”) + -lös (“-less”), from Old Swedish sakløs, Old Norse saklauss. Compare Danish sagesløs (“blameless”), Icelandic saklaus (“innocent”), English sackless.

parole.significato: to miss, to lack, to want, to be without
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sakna, from Old Norse sakna (“miss”).

parole.significato: a large room, a hall (often for more-or-less public activities)
parole.testo: From Old Norse salr, from Proto-Germanic *saliz, from Proto-Indo-European *sol-, *sel-.
From Old Swedish salter, from Old Norse saltr, from Proto-Germanic *saltaz, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l, *sáls.

From Old Swedish salt, from Old Norse salt (akin to Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌻𐍄 (salt), Old English sealt, Old High German salz, Old Saxon salt), from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Cognate with Danish, Icelandic, and Norwegian salt.
From Old Swedish salta, from Old Norse salta, from Proto-Germanic *saltaną.
Inherited from Old Norse sam- (“together, con-”).

parole.significato: an association, a community, a society (especially a religious one)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish samfunder, from Old Norse samfundr, equivalent to sam- (“co-”) + fund (“meeting, get-together”).

parole.significato: a society; a long-standing group of people sharing cultural aspects
parole.testo: From Old Norse samheldi, equivalent to sam- + hålla. Doublet of samhäll.

parole.significato: to collect, to gather, to organize
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sambla, from Old Norse samna, from Proto-Germanic *samnōną.
From Old Norse samr, from Proto-Germanic *samaz, from Proto-Indo-European *somHós.
From Old Norse saman.
From Old Swedish sander, from Old Norse sandr, from Proto-Germanic *samdaz.
From Old Swedish sander, from Old Norse sannr, from Proto-Germanic *sanþaz. Cognate of English sooth.
Inherited from Old Swedish sannind, sannindi, from Old Norse sannind. Cognate of Icelandic sannindi. By surface analysis, sann + -ing.
From Old Swedish sax (“single-bevel knife”), from Old Norse sax (“big work knife”), from Proto-Germanic *sahsą, from Proto-Indo-European *sek-.
From Old Norse skarlak, which came via Middle Low German [Term?] from Medieval Latin scarlatum, probably from Arabic سِقِرْلَاط (siqirlāṭ), a variant of سِقِلّاط (siqillāṭ, “scarlet cloth”).
From Old Swedish sēa, sē, sīa, from Old Norse séa, sjá, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną. Final -g of the past tense form added under influence of the Old Swedish plural form sāgho.

parole.significato: custom (general (traditional) deliberate habit of some group of people)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish siþer, from Old Norse siðr, from Proto-Germanic *siduz.

parole.significato: then, after this (that), afterwards; next in order
parole.testo: From Old Swedish siþan, from Old Norse síðan. See Norwegian siden. Cognate with Old English siþþan.
From Old Swedish siþvänia, siþvania, from Old Norse siðvenja. By surface analysis, sed + vänja.

parole.significato: sail; a piece of fabric attached to a boat
parole.testo: From Old Norse segl, from Proto-Germanic *seglą.
From Old Norse sigr (“victory”), from Proto-Germanic *segaz.
From Old Swedish sighla, from Old Norse sigla, from Proto-Germanic *siglijaną.

parole.significato: to win; to obtain a victory
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sighra, from Old Norse sigra (“to win”), from Proto-Germanic *sigizōną. Equivalent to seger (“victory”) + -a.
From Old Norse seinn (“late”).
Inherited from Old Swedish sina, from Old Norse sina, sin, from Proto-Germanic *sinwō.
Inherited from Old Swedish sæx, siæx, from Old Norse sex, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs (“six”).
From Old Swedish sæxtan, siæxtān, from Old Norse sextán, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun.

parole.significato: to foretell; to tell the future
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sīa, sēa, from Old Norse sjá, from Proto-Germanic *sehwaną.

parole.significato: side; a bounding straight edge or surface
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sīþa, from Old Norse síða, from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ.

parole.significato: reflexive case of han, hon, den, det, de or man; compare himself, herself, itself, themselves, oneself
parole.testo: From Old Norse sik, from Proto-Germanic *sek, from Proto-Indo-European *se.
From Old Norse síld, from Proto-Germanic *sīlą.
Inherited from Old Swedish silver, from Old Norse silfr, from Proto-Germanic *silubrą.
From Old Norse svimma, from Proto-Germanic *swimmaną.

parole.significato: his (own), her (own), its (own), their (own). (Reflexive possessive third person pronoun)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sīn, from Old Norse sínn, from Proto-Germanic *sīnaz. Cognate with Danish sin, Gothic 𐍃𐌴𐌹𐌽𐍃 (seins), German sein, Dutch zijn.

parole.significato: to slow down or delay (someone or something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish senka, from Old Norse seinka, to the same root as sen (“late”).

From Old Swedish sizter (adjective), Old Swedish sizt (adverb), from Old Norse síztr (adjective), sízt (adverb), superlatives of an adjective related to Old Norse síðr (adjective), Old Norse síð (“late”, adverb); hence Danish sidst (Old Danish sist, Norwegian sist).
From Old Norse síðastr. By surface analysis, sist + -a.

parole.significato: to sit (be in a position with the upper body upright and the legs resting)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sitia, from Old Norse sitja, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.
From Old Swedish siu, syū, from Old Norse sjau, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
From Old Swedish siūþa, from Old Norse sjúða (Old West Norse sjóða), from Proto-Germanic *seuþaną. Cognate with German sieden, English seethe and Old English sēoþan.
From Old Swedish siūker, from Old Norse sjúkr, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz.
From Old Norse sjúkdómr, sjuk + dom.
From Old Swedish siundi, from Old Norse sjaundi, from Proto-Germanic *sebundô. Doublet of syvende, which was borrowed from Danish.
From Old Swedish siunga, from Old Norse syngva, syngja, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-.
From Old Swedish siutan‚ siuttān, from Old Norse sjaután, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun.

parole.significato: oneself, myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself
parole.testo: From Old Norse sjalfr, from Proto-Germanic *selbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *selbʰ- (“one's own”), from *s(w)e- (“separate, apart”).
From Old Swedish sætti, from Old Norse sétti, from Proto-Germanic *sehtô.
From Old Swedish siœr, from Old Norse sær, from Proto-Germanic *saiwiz. Cognate with Dutch zee, English sea, German See.

parole.significato: scabies (An infestation of parasitic mites, Sarcoptes scabiei)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skabber, from Old Norse skabb, from Proto-Germanic *skabbaz, from Proto-Indo-European *skabn-, *skab- (“to cut, split, carve, shape”). Cognate with Latin scabiēs.

parole.significato: scathe; damage (abstract measure of something not being intact), an injury, a harm, a wound
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skaþi, from Old Norse skaði, from Proto-Germanic *skaþô, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keh₁t-. Cognate to English scathe.

parole.significato: scathe; to injure, to harm, to hurt, to damage, to wound
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skaþa, from Old Norse skaða, from Proto-Germanic *skaþōną. Cognate to English scathe.

parole.significato: a handle, a grip, a shaft (long thin handle, on for example a broom, knife, paintbrush, or pipe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish skaft, skapt, from Old Norse skapt, skaft, from Proto-Germanic *skaftaz. Doublet of schakt and skäkta.

parole.significato: to shake (physically or to disturb emotionally)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skaka, from Old Norse skaka (“to shake”), from Proto-Germanic *skakaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kek- (“to shake, stir”). Cognate with Norwegian skake, Danish skage, Icelandic skaka, Low German schaken and English shake.

parole.significato: trace, tug (rod that connects a cart with the harness on each side of the draft animal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish skakul, from Old Norse skǫkull, from Proto-Germanic *skakulaz. Cognate of English shackle. Doublet of schackel.

parole.significato: shell ((hard) external covering of an animal, egg, nut, various objects, etc. – used similarly to English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skal, from Old Norse skel, from Proto-Germanic *skaljō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cleave”). Compare Danish skæl, Dutch schaal, Dutch schil, English shale, English shell, German Schale, Norwegian skjell.
Learned borrowing from Old Norse skald. The inherited form would be *skåll.
skald (“a poet”) + -a. The first being a learned borrowing from Old Norse skáld (“a poet”).

parole.significato: a loud or shrill and widely audible sound or noise of any kind, especially such that produces an echo
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skal, from Old Norse skall n, skǫll f, to the verb Old Norse skjalla (“clash, clatter”), from Proto-Germanic *skellaną or *skellǭ, originally “to sound (strong)” and thereof. Cognate to Old Danish skald, Norwegian Nynorsk skoll; Middle Low German schal; Old High German scal, German
From Old Norse skalli.
From Old Swedish skam, from Old Norse skǫmm, from Proto-Germanic *skamō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European.

parole.significato: to create; to make, to manufacture; to put into existence, chiefly by a creative act
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skapa, from Old Norse skapa (“to create”), from Proto-Germanic *skapjaną. Related to German schaffen and English shape.

parole.significato: a group of people (physically or more abstractly together)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skǫr, from Proto-Germanic *skarō (“division, portion”).
From Old Swedish skarper, from Old Norse skarpr, from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerb-, from *(s)ker- (“to cut”).
From Old Norse skarfr, from a Germanic base imitative of the birds' harsh croaking sounds.

From Old Swedish skata, from Old Norse skata, derivative of Old Norse skade (“top, cliff, tree top”; compare Swedish: skate, skati, “tip, top, tree top”), probably more directly “shoot” (cf. Swedish utskott (“protuberance”)), referencing their long tails. The word is possibly related to Old Norse sk
From Old Norse skattr, from Proto-Germanic *skattaz, from Proto-Indo-European *skat-·.

parole.significato: to chafe, to rub, to scrape
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skava, from Old Norse skafa, from Proto-Germanic *skabaną, from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”).
From Old Swedish skedh, from Old Norse skeið. Compare Danish ske, Norwegian Bokmål skje, Norwegian Nynorsk skei.

parole.significato: a stage, a phase (delimited part of something that happens)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skeið (“race; race course; piece of way; space of time”), from Proto-Germanic *skaiþaną (“to separate”).
From Old Swedish skip, from Old Norse skip, from Proto-Germanic *skipą. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from Latin navis.
From Old Norse skíð (“snowshoe, billet”), from Proto-Germanic *skīdą (“billet”).

parole.significato: to separate; to cause to be separate
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skilia, from Old Norse skilja, from Proto-Germanic *skiljaną (“to separate, limit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to split, cut”).
From Old Swedish skillinger, from Old Norse skillingr, from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz, the same source of English shilling.
From Old Swedish skilnadher, from Old Norse skilnaðr.

parole.significato: more or less splendid or special attire; attire, garb, dress, (when a robe) robe

parole.significato: tail for swimming (tail of a fish, seal, whale, snake, crustacean, even beaver)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sporþer, from Old Norse sporðr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)prend- (“to spring, rush”), see also Proto-Slavic *prę̀dati (“to jump, leap”). Cognate to Norwegian Nynorsk spol, spor, spord.
From Old Norse spóla, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ.
From Old Norse spori, from Proto-Germanic *spurô.

parole.significato: a crack, a fracture; a thin and usually jagged space opened in a previously solid material
parole.testo: From Old Swedish springa, from Old Norse springa, from Proto-Germanic *springaną.
From Old Swedish springa, from Old Norse springa, from Proto-Germanic *springaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sprenǵʰ-.

parole.significato: something that emits a jet of liquid (or several); a sprayer, a squirt
parole.testo: From Old Norse sprúta, from Proto-Germanic *spreutaną.

parole.significato: speckled (with irregular spots or blotches (or stripes, etc.) of two or more colors)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish spräklotter, from Old Norse spreklóttr. Cognate of Danish spraglet, Middle High German spreckeleht, English spreckled. Possibly from the same root as in English sprinkle.

parole.significato: to blow up, to blast (make (something) explode)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sprængia, from Old Norse sprengja, from Proto-Germanic *sprangijaną, causative of Proto-Germanic *springaną. Doublet of springa.

parole.significato: to throw up, to puke, to vomit
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spȳia, spȳa, spȳ, from Old Norse spýja, from Proto-Germanic *spīwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ptyēw- (“to spit, vomit”). Compare Norwegian and Danish spy, Icelandic spýja, English spew, Dutch spuwen, German speien.

parole.significato: to dilute (add a fluid (often water) to another fluid to make it less strong)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spædhia, from Old Norse spað (“meat soup”). Cognate with Danish spæde and Swedish späd; compare with the English verb thin (in the sense "dilute").

parole.significato: to tighten, to tense (make tense or taut, of muscles, a rope, a spring, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish spänna, from Old Norse spenna, from Proto-Germanic *spannijaną, causative of *spannaną (“to stretch, to span”). Cognate with Danish spænde, and Middle Low German spennen.
From Old Swedish spänne, from Old Norse spenni, from the verb spenni (“to stretch”), from Proto-Germanic *spannijaną, cognate with Danish spænde.

parole.significato: stop, catch, block, blockade, ban, limit, bar, lock (something stopping or hindering)
parole.testo: From Old Norse sperra, from Proto-Germanic *sparrijaną.
From Old Norse sparri, from Proto-Germanic *sparrô (“log, wooden beam”).

parole.significato: to foretell, to divine; to tell the future and fortune through supernatural means
parole.testo: From Old Norse spá (“to foretell, prophesy”), from Proto-Germanic *spahōną, *spēhōną (“to observe”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

parole.significato: a thin planed- or ground off piece of wood or (more rarely) iron or the like; a shaving, a chip
parole.testo: From Old Norse spánn (“shaving, chip”)

parole.significato: A puncheon bridge (a narrow bridge for one walking person (not wide enough for two to meet))
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse spǫng. Cognate with Danish spang (with the same meaning) and Icelandic spöng.

parole.significato: a trail or trace; a mark left by something that has passed along or happened, also figuratively
parole.testo: From Old Norse spor, from Proto-Germanic *spurą.

From Old Swedish spyria, from Old Norse spyrja, from Proto-Germanic *spurjaną. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål spørre, Norwegian Nynorsk spørje, spørja, Danish spørge, Icelandic spyrja, Faroese spyrja, Dutch speuren, German spüren, Luxembourgish spieren, English speer, speir, spere and Scots speir.
From Old Norse spyrna

parole.significato: a stack (e.g. of hay), a pile (e.g. of manure)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stakkr, from Proto-Germanic *stakkaz.

From Old Swedish staþer, from Old Norse staðr, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis. The sense “town, city” is a semantic loan from Middle Low German stat, from the same Proto-Germanic noun.
Inherited from Old Swedish stag, from Old Norse stag, from Proto-Germanic *stagą.
From Old Swedish staki, from Old Norse staki, from Proto-Germanic *stakô, from Proto-Indo-European *steg-.
From Old Swedish stalder, from Old Norse stallr.
From Old Swedish stalder, from Old Norse stallr, from Proto-Germanic *stallaz.

Inherited from Old Swedish stalbrodhir, from Old Norse stallbróðir, from Middle Low German stalbrōder, likely a calque of Medieval Latin constabularius. By surface analysis, stall (“stable”) + broder (“brother”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk stallbror.
From Old Swedish staffn, stampn, from Old Norse stafn. Cognate with Danish stavn.

parole.significato: to stutter, to stammer (have a stutter or currently stutter, for any reason)
parole.testo: Old Swedish stama, from Old Norse stama. Cognate of Icelandic stama and Danish stamme. Compare with German stammeln, English stammer.
From Old Swedish stampa, from Old Norse stampa (Compare Old West Norse stappa), all from Proto-Germanic *stampōną.

parole.significato: to stay; to remain at a place
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stadhna, from Old Norse staðna, derived from the past participle staðinn.
From Old Norse stǫpull (“column, pillar”).
From Old Norse stari, from Proto-Germanic *staraz, from Proto-Indo-European *storo- (“starling”) or *(s)tern- (“starling”), same ultimate source as Old Prussian starnite (“gull”).

parole.significato: strong (capable of producing great physical force)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish starker, from Old Norse starkr, from Proto-Germanic *starkuz, from Proto-Indo-European *sterg-.
From Old Swedish staver, from Old Norse stafr, from Proto-Norse ᛋᛏᛡᛒᛡ (staba), from Proto-Germanic *stabaz.

parole.significato: to spell (to give the individual letters of a word)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stava, from Old Norse stafa, equivalent to stav (“letter”) + -a.

parole.significato: a step (with the foot, sometimes figuratively)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stig. Cognate with Norwegian steg, Icelandic stig, Faroese stig.
From Old Norse stigi and stegi. Cognate with Icelandic stigi.

parole.significato: a steak, a roast, a joint (meat)
parole.testo: From Old Norse steik.

parole.significato: to fry: to cook (something) in hot fat
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stekia, from Old Norse steikja.

From Old Swedish stirder, styrdher, from Old Norse stirðr, from Proto-Germanic *sterþjaz, [Term?], from Proto-Indo-European *ster (“strong, steady”). From Old Swedish stirdhna, from Old Norse stirðna.
From Old Swedish sten, from Old Norse steinn, from Proto-Norse ᛊᛏᚨᛁᚾᚨᛉ (stainaʀ), from Proto-Germanic *stainaz, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂-.

parole.significato: a sty (pen or enclosure for swine)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stía, stí, from Proto-Germanic *stiją, which could be ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steyh₂- (“to stiffen”), similar to *stainaz (“stone”). Cognate of Icelandic stía, English sty.
Old Norse stikka, from Proto-Germanic *stikkô, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg-, related to Etymology 2 below. Compare Icelandic stika, English stick.
Old Norse stika, from Proto-Germanic *stikaną. Compare Danish stikke, German stechen, English stick

parole.significato: a path, a trail (in nature and narrow)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stīgher, from Old Norse stígr. Cognate with Danish sti and German Steig. Related to Swedish stiga. See also Old English stig.

parole.significato: to step; to move the foot in walking
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stīgha, from Old Norse stíga, from Proto-Germanic *stīganą. Cognate with Danish stige, Norwegian stige, English sty, German steigen, Dutch stijgen.
From Old Swedish stilla, from Old Norse stilla, borrowed from Middle Low German stillen, from Old Saxon *stillian, from Proto-West Germanic *stillijan.

parole.significato: a school, a shoal (large group of fish (or other sea creatures) swimming together)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stim, from Old Norse stím, ultimately from a root meaning "to hang together, stand," from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”).
From Old Swedish stinga, from Old Norse stinga, from Proto-Germanic *stinganą. Compare Icelandic and Faroese stinga, English sting.
From Old Norse stíra.
Inherited from Old Swedish stiæla, from Old Norse stela, from Proto-Germanic *stelaną.

parole.significato: to tip over, to topple (usually a vessel containing a liquid)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stiælpa, from Old Norse stelpa, from Proto-Germanic *stalpijaną, causative of *stelpaną.
From Old Swedish stiærna, from Old Norse stjarna, from Proto-Germanic *sternǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.

parole.significato: a bottom, a behind, a butt
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stiærter, stærter, from Old Norse stertr, from Proto-Germanic *stertaz.
From Old Swedish stōþ, from Old Norse stóð, from Proto-Germanic *stōdą. Compare Icelandic stóð.

parole.significato: a log (trunk of a dead tree)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stokker, from Old Norse stokkr, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“tree-trunk”).
From Old Swedish stōl, from Old Norse stóll, from Proto-Germanic *stōlaz, from Proto-Indo-European *stāl- (“frame, rack, stand”).
From Old Swedish stolpe, from Old Norse stolpi, from Proto-Germanic *stulpô, related to *stallaz (“stable, standing, stall”).

From Old Swedish stolter (“majestic, beautiful, fine, proud”), from Old Norse stoltr, from Proto-Germanic *stultaz. See also Danish stolt, Middle Low German stolt, Middle High German and present German stolz.

parole.significato: a beer mug, a stein, a tankard, especially of metal
parole.testo: From Old Norse staup (“small glass for liquor”).
From Old Norse stoppa, from Middle Low German stoppen, from Old Saxon *stoppon, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn.
From Old Swedish stōr, from Old Norse stórr (“big, large, tall, great”), from Proto-Germanic *stōraz, from Proto-Indo-European *stāro-.
Inherited from Old Swedish storker, from Old Norse storkr.

parole.significato: storm; heavy winds or weather associated with storm winds.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stormber, from Old Norse stormr, from Proto-Germanic *sturmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).
From Old Swedish strand, from Old Norse strǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *strandō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)trAnt-.

parole.significato: rapid, swift, rich (of a stream or rain)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stríðr.
From Old Swedish stridh, from Old Norse stríð.
Inherited from Old Norse stríða, from Proto-Germanic *strīdaną
From Old Norse stríðsmaðr. Compound of strid + -s- + man.

parole.significato: throat (front part of the neck; gullet; windpipe)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish strūpe, from Old Norse strúpi, strjúpi, from Proto-Germanic [Term?]. Cognate with Danish strube, Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk strupe and Icelandic strjúpi.

parole.significato: to strike (out), to erase, to delete, to remove (strike out, often figuratively)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish strȳka, from Old Norse strjúka, from Proto-Germanic *streukaną.
From Old Norse strangr, from Proto-Germanic *strangaz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ- (“taut”).

parole.significato: a string (kept or intended to be kept taut, for example on an instrument, bow, or racket)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish strænger, from Old Norse strengr, from Proto-Germanic *strangiz, from Proto-Indo-European *strengʰ-.

parole.significato: a stalk of a grass or sedge (whether growing or dried)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stra, from Old Norse strá, from Proto-Germanic *strawą. Related to English straw.
From Old Swedish strø̄ia, from Old Norse strá, from Proto-Germanic *strawjaną.
From Old Swedish strömber, from Old Norse straumr, from Proto-Germanic *straumaz, from Proto-Indo-European *srówmos, from *srew- (“to flow”).

parole.significato: to flow, to stream (run in great quantities, of liquid, or other things by extension)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse streyma. Compare Faroese streyma, Norwegian Nynorsk strøyma, Danish strømme.
From Old Norse stubbi, from Proto-Germanic *stubbô.

parole.significato: a cottage, a cabin (small (wooden) house (in the countryside))
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stuva, stova, stugha, from Old Norse stofa, stufa, borrowed from Middle Low German stōve, stūve, Old Saxon *stova, *stuva, from Proto-West Germanic *stobu. Cognate with English stove. Also related to Finnish tupa. The change from v > g is due to a dialectal development from -β- > -w

parole.significato: a stump (something which has been cut off or continuously shortened, like for example as a very short pencil or what is…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stumper, from Old Norse stumpr, from Proto-Germanic *stumpaz.
From Old Norse stund, from Proto-Germanic *stundō (“point in time, hour”), from Proto-Indo-European *stut- (“prop”), from Proto-Indo-European *stā-, *sth- (“to stand”).
From Old Norse stútr, from Proto-Germanic *stautōną. Cognate with Danish stud, Norwegian stut, and English stot.

parole.significato: a piece (part of something, a part of a distance)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stykki, from Proto-Germanic *stukkiją, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewg-. Cognate with Old English stycce and German Stück.

parole.significato: naughty, mean, bad ((inclined towards) misbehaving or acting badly)
parole.testo: Derived from Old Swedish stygger, from Old Norse styggr.
From Old Swedish stȳra, from Old Norse stýra, from Proto-Germanic *stiurijaną.
From Old Norse stýri.
From Old Swedish styrkia, from Old Norse styrkja, from styrkr (“strong”).

parole.significato: step-; in family relations, represents incompleteness, sharing just one parent
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stiūp-, stiūf-, from the Old Norse stjúp-, from Proto-Germanic *steupa- (“orphaned, step-”).
From Old Swedish stæþ, variant of stæþi, from Old Norse steði.

From Old Swedish stǣþia, from Old Norse steðja (“stop, affirm, permit”), from Proto-Germanic *stadiz (“place, location”), from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis (“standing, position”). Cognate with Icelandic steðja, Faroese steðga, Norwegian ste and stede, Danish stede. Doublet of städa and stad.

parole.significato: to close, to shut (a door, hatch, border, space, or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Norse stengja (“to bar”) (> Danish stænge (“to bar, bolt”)), cognate with dialectal German stängen/stängeln.

parole.significato: to splash with scattered drops or a small amount of some liquid, to spatter, to sprinkle
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stænkia, from Old Norse støkkva, from Proto-Germanic *stankwijaną, causative of *stinkwaną (whence Swedish stinka). Cognate with Danish stænke.

From Old Norse stefja (“to prevent”), likely borrowed at a late stage rather than inherited. Arguably related to steðja (“to stop”) and thus from Proto-Germanic *stadiz. More likely related to stav (“staff; rod”), and thus from Proto-Germanic *stabaz.

From Old Norse stál, from Proto-Germanic *stahlą, from Proto-Indo-European *stak- (“to stay, be firm”). Compare Danish and Norwegian stål, Icelandic stál, Dutch staal, German Stahl, also English steel.

parole.significato: to be held, to take place, to happen
parole.testo: From Old Swedish standa, from Old Norse standa. Cognate with Danish stande, Icelandic standa and Norwegian Nynorsk standa.

parole.testo: From Old Swedish stang, from Old Norse stǫng, from Proto-Germanic *stangō. Cognate with Icelandic stöng.

parole.significato: to pant and moan (as after exertion)

From late Old Swedish stydh, from earlier Old Swedish stuþ, stoþ, from Old Norse stoð, stuð, from Proto-Germanic *stuþs, from Proto-Indo-European *stut-. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stew- (“be firm”).
From Late Old Swedish stødhia, from Old Swedish styþia, from Old Norse styðja, from Proto-Germanic *stuþjaną.

parole.testo: From Old Swedish stynia, from Old Norse stynja. Cognate of Danish stønne, German stöhnen, English stun.

parole.significato: a pole, chiefly used in the construction of roundpole fences
parole.testo: From Old Swedish stør, from Old Norse staur (Old Gutnish dialect), from Proto-Germanic *staura-, from Ancient Greek σταυρός (staurós) (hence Latin restaurare, hence French restaurer).

parole.significato: to put down poles into the ground
parole.testo: From Old Norse staura.

parole.significato: a sharp impact (or the resulting shock through something); an impact, a shock, a jolt, a bump, a knock, etc.

From Old Swedish støvel, from Old Norse styfill, from Middle Low German stevele, stovele, from Italian stivale, from Medieval Latin aestivale.
Related to suga (“to suck”), both from Old Norse súga.

parole.significato: a booby (bird of the Sula genus and/or Sulidae family)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse súla, related to svala; both are from Proto-Germanic *swalwǭ.

parole.testo: From Old Norse sund, from Proto-Germanic *sundą, from Proto-Indo-European *sm̥tóm.

parole.significato: to drink hard liquor (to get drunk and often excessively); to drink, to booze
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sūpa, from Old Norse súpa, from Proto-Germanic *sūpaną.

parole.significato: sour (having the characteristic taste of for example a lemon or vinegar)

Inherited from Old Norse svanr, from Proto-Germanic *swanaz (“swan”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”).
From Old Norse svar (“answer, reply”).

parole.testo: From Old Norse svara (“to answer”), from Proto-Germanic *swarōną, cognate to English answer. Compare svar (“a response”).

parole.significato: Swedes (members of a North Germanic tribe)

From Old Swedish svik, Old Norse svik, from Proto-Germanic *swiką.

parole.significato: Swedish; of or pertaining to Sweden or the Swedish language
parole.testo: From Old Norse svenskr, sœnskr, from Proto-Germanic *swihaniskaz (“Swedish”), from *swihô (“Swede”).

parole.significato: to sweep (move in a sweeping motion)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svepa, swæpa, from Old Norse sveipa, from Proto-Germanic *swaipaną.
From Old Norse sveiti, from Proto-Germanic *swait-, *swaitô, from Proto-Indo-European *swoyd- (“to sweat”), *sweyd-.

parole.significato: to sting, to burn (hurt with a continuous, sharp (often somewhat queasy) pain, like after getting stung by nettles, rub…

parole.significato: to betray, to let down, to disappoint
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svīkia, from Old Norse svíkja, from Proto-Germanic *swīkwaną.

From Old Swedish svælgha, from Old Norse svelga, svelgja, from Proto-Germanic *swelganą, from Proto-Indo-European *swelk-.

parole.significato: to swell (become bigger, especially due to being engorged)

parole.significato: to starve, to hunger (be the victim of famine or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish svælta, from Old Norse svelta, from Proto-Germanic *sweltaną.

parole.testo: From Old Swedish svær, from Old Norse *svær, from Proto-Germanic *swehuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros (“father-in-law”).

From Old Norse *sverta, from Proto-Germanic *swartijaną.

parole.significato: difficult, hard (requiring significant effort (or luck or the like) to successfully deal with)
