parole.testo: From Old Norse sýna, related to Old Norse sjá.
From Old Norse synd, from Proto-Germanic *sundijō; compare Old English synn (modern English sin).
From Old Swedish syndogher, from Old Norse syndugr, equivalent to synd (“sin”) + -ig (“-y”). Compare English sinny.
syn + -lig or from Old Norse sýnn, sýniligr.
From Old Norse sýra.
From Old Swedish systkin, systkon, systkan, syskane, söszkone, from Old Norse systkin‚ from Runic Swedish systgini.

parole.significato: something (productive) one (often regularly) does; an occupation (in the more general, not-necessarily-job sense), a ch…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sȳsla, from Old Norse sýsla, from Proto-Germanic *seuhslō.

parole.significato: a sister (woman or girl having the same parents)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish systir, from Old Norse systir, from Proto-Norse ᛊᚹᛖᛊᛏᚨᚱ (swestar), from Proto-Germanic *swestēr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr (“sister”).
From Old Norse sekkr, from Proto-Germanic *sakkuz (“sack”), from Latin saccus (“large bag”), from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “bag of coarse cloth”), from Semitic.

parole.significato: grain (grass food crops, generically, as a "substance")
parole.testo: From Old Norse sáð (“seed”), from Proto-Germanic *sēdiz.

From Old Swedish sæghia, sighia, from Old Norse segja, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sekʷ-. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål si, Norwegian Nynorsk seie, Danish sige, German sagen and English say.

parole.significato: a folk legend (usually containing supernatural elements and claiming to be true)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sæghn, saghn, from Old Norse sǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *sagnō, cognate with Danish sagn, Old English sæġen (“saying, statement”). Derived from *sagjaną (“to say”).
From Old Norse selr (“seal”).
From Old Norse selja.
From Old Swedish sælia, from Old Norse selja (“sell”), from Proto-Germanic *saljaną.
From Old Swedish sæll, from Old Norse sæll (“happy”), from Proto-Germanic *sēliz. Cognate of Icelandic sæll.
From Old Swedish siäldan, säldan, siällan, from Old Norse sjaldan, Proto-Germanic *seldanē.

parole.significato: harmony, friendship, people (or animals) getting along
parole.testo: From Old Norse semja (“to get along”), from Proto-Germanic *samjaną.

parole.significato: to send, to transmit (make something go somewhere)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sænda, from Old Norse senda, from Proto-Germanic *sandijaną.

parole.significato: a bed (piece of furniture to sleep in)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish siang, from Old Norse sæing (“bed”), later sæng.
From Old Swedish sænkia, from Old Norse sænkva, (Old West Norse søkkva) from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną.
From Old Swedish sær, from Old Norse sér, dative of sik (Swedish sig).

parole.significato: a shift, a chemise, a smock (type of (woman's) undergarment (made of linen or the like), similar to a long-sleeved shir…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish særker, from Old Norse serkr, from Proto-Germanic *sarkiz (“shirt, armour, hauberk”), from Proto-Indo-European *swerg-, *swerk- (“clothes worn outside”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to arrange, tack, tie, unite”). Cognate with Scots sark, serk (“shirt, shift”), North Frisian se
From Old Norse sæti, from Proto-Germanic *sētiją.

parole.significato: to sit; to move oneself into a sitting position
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sætia, from Old Norse setja, from Proto-Germanic *satjaną. Cognate with English set.

parole.significato: so, like that, in such a way
parole.testo: From Old Norse svá, from Proto-Germanic *swa, *swē.

parole.significato: a tub, especially one for animals to drink from
parole.testo: From Old Norse sár, from Proto-Germanic *saihaz.
From Old Swedish sā, from Old Norse sá, from Proto-Germanic *sēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-.

parole.significato: a saw (tool with a toothed blade used for cutting hard substances, in particular wood or metal)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sagh, saagh (Late Old Swedish), from Old Norse sǫg, from Proto-Germanic *sagō, from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”).
From Old Swedish sānger, from Old Norse sǫngr, from Proto-Germanic *sangwaz.

parole.significato: to rub with soft soap (especially to make very slippery)
parole.testo: From late Old Norse sápa, from Old English sāpe, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ.

parole.significato: a wound, a puncture of the skin or a mucous membrane
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sar, from Old Norse sár, from Proto-Germanic *sairą.
Inherited from Old Swedish sātter, from Old Norse sáttr (“reconciled”), from Proto-Germanic *sahtaz.

Inherited from Late Old Swedish sø̄der, sø̄dher, sudher, from Old Norse suðr, with the ø-umlaut from södre, Old Swedish syþre, Old Norse syðri (comparative); compare the ø in Norwegian sør, Danish sønder. Doublet of syd. Compare dialectal Danish sønder, Old Norse sunnr, Old High German sundar. Other

parole.significato: to search (look throughout (a place) for something), to seek
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sø̄kia, sökia, from Old Norse sǿkja, from Proto-Germanic *sōkijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“to seek out”).
From Old Norse saumr, from sýja (“to sew”).
From Old Swedish symn, sømn, from Old Norse svefn, from Proto-Germanic *swefnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *swep- (“sleep”).

parole.significato: Sunday (now generally considered the seventh day of the week in non-religious contexts in Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish sunnodagher, from Old Norse sunnudagr, borrowed from a West Germanic language. Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *sunnōn dag, a calque of Latin diēs Sōlis.

parole.significato: to grieve, to mourn (usually someone's death)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish syrghia, from Old Norse syrgja, from Proto-Germanic *surgijaną.
From Old Swedish söter, from Old Norse sœtr, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, from Proto-Indo-European *swéh₂dus. Compare English sweet, German süß.
From Old Norse sœtr, from Proto-Germanic *swōtuz, from Proto-Indo-European *sweh₂dus. Compare Icelandic sætur (“sweet”) and its neuter form sætt.

parole.significato: send to sleep, cause someone to fall asleep
parole.testo: From Old Norse sœfa, sǿfa, causative of sova (< sofa).

parole.significato: take; to grab and move to oneself
parole.testo: Apocopic form of taga, from Old Swedish taka, from Old Norse taka, from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną. Cognate with English take.

From Old Swedish þak, from Runic Swedish þakk, from Old Norse þǫkk, from Proto-Germanic *þankō, *þankaz. Cognates include English thank, German Dank, Danish tak and Norwegian Nynorsk takk/Norwegian Bokmål takk.
From Old Swedish þakka, from Old Norse þakka, from Proto-Germanic *þankōną.

parole.significato: to grope (touch sexually), usually against someone's will
parole.testo: From Old Norse tafsa, variant of Old Norse tapsa (“to tap”), likely to Proto-Germanic *tabōną. Compare Faroese tava, Norwegian Nynorsk tava, English tap, German tappen (“to grope”), etc.
From Old Norse tak.
From Old Swedish þak, from Old Norse þak, from Proto-Germanic *þaką, from Proto-Indo-European *teg-.
From Old Swedish tal, from Old Norse tal, from Proto-Germanic *talą.
From Old Norse tala, from Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to tell, count”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to reckon, count”).

parole.significato: pine, Scots pine tree, Pinus sylvestris
parole.testo: From Old Norse þǫll. Cognate with Jamtish toll, Icelandic þöll.
From Old Swedish tamber, from Old Norse tamr, from Proto-Germanic *tamaz, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.
From Old Swedish tan, from Old Norse tǫnn, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts.
From Old Swedish tapper, from Old Norse tappi, from Proto-Germanic *tappô (“tap, plug”), see also English tap, Danish tap.
From Old Norse tapa (“to lose”). In the sense “to tap” from Middle Low German tappen.
From Old Swedish tharmber, from Old Norse þarmr.
From Old Swedish þarf, from Old Norse þǫrf (“need”). Cognate with Old English þearf, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐍂𐌱𐌰 (þarba) and Icelandic þörf. Doublet of torft.
Inherited from Old Swedish þorva, þarva, from Old Norse þurfa, from Proto-Germanic *þurbaną.
From Old Swedish tafla, from Old Norse tafla, ultimately from Latin tabula via Low German. Doublet of tavle, tavel, and tabell, and related to tablett, tablå, tävla.
From Old Swedish tēa, from Old Norse tjá, from Proto-Germanic *tīhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-. Cognate of Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍄𐌴𐌹𐌷𐌰𐌽 (gateihan), German zeihen, Dutch tijgen.

parole.significato: a small farm field, a part of a larger field
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tegher, from Old Norse teigr.

parole.significato: brick (burned clay, the material, used for roof tiles and bricks), tiles
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tighl, from Old Norse tigl, from Proto-Germanic *tigulǭ. Same as Icelandic tigl, Danish tegel, Old English tigele, English tile, Middle Low German tegel, German Ziegel, Latin tegula, a form of tegere (“to cover”) (a roof with tiles), relating to Swedish tak (“roof”) and täcka (“to c
Likely onomatopoeic, from the sound of the bird. Inherited from Old Norse þeisti, from Proto-Germanic *þaistô.
From Old Swedish ten, from Old Norse teinn (“sprout, twig, branch”), from Proto-Germanic *tainaz
From Old Swedish tin, ten, from Old Norse tin, from Proto-Germanic *tiną.
Inherited from Old Swedish tiþ, from Old Norse tíð, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis.

parole.significato: early (at a time in advance of the usual or expected event)
parole.testo: From Old Norse tíðligr and Middle Low German tidelik, related to tid.
Possibly from Old Norse tíðindi (“tidings”)

parole.significato: to refrain from saying anything, to keep silent, to stay silent
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þighia, from Old Norse þegja, from Proto-Germanic *þagjaną.
From Old Swedish þiggia, from Old Norse þiggja (“to receive”), from Proto-Germanic *þigjaną.
From Old Norse tík (“bitch”). Compare English tyke.
From Old Swedish til, from Old Norse til, from Proto-Germanic *til (compare *tilą (“goal”)).
From Old Norse til sǫlu.

parole.significato: an hour (time period of sixty minutes)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tīme, from Old Norse tími, from Proto-Germanic *tīmô (“time”), from Proto-Germanic *tī-, from Proto-Indo-European *dī- (“time”).

parole.significato: timber, log to be used in construction
parole.testo: From Old Norse timbr.
From Old Swedish þing, from Old Norse þing (“assembly, council, business”), from Proto-Germanic *þingą.
From Old Norse tíu, from Proto-Germanic *tehun (“ten”), from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥ (“ten”). Cognate with Icelandic tíu, Faroese tíggju, Norwegian ti, Danish ti and English ten.
From Old Swedish tiundi, from Old Norse tíundi, from Proto-Germanic *tehundô.

parole.significato: Tuesday (now generally considered the second day of the week in non-religious contexts in Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tisdagher, from an East Norse variant *tísdagr of Old Norse týsdagr, from Proto-West Germanic *Tīwas dag (the rounding of the *-ī- to -ý- due to the following *-w- is a West Norse development), a calque of Latin dies Martis.
From Old Norse þistill.
From Old Swedish thiokker, thiukker, from Old Norse þykkr, þjukkr, þjokkr, from Proto-Germanic *þekuz, from Proto-Indo-European *tégus.
From Old Norse þjóð (“people, nation”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō, from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“tribe”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌸𐌹𐌿𐌳𐌰 (þiuda) and Icelandic þjóð.
From Old Swedish tiugher, from Old Norse tigr, tøgr, from Proto-Germanic *teguz (“group of ten”). Doublet of -tio.

parole.significato: tether (for binding cattle to a pole or the like)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tiūþer, from Old Norse tjóðr, from Proto-Germanic *teudrą. Cognate with German Low German Tüder, English tether.

parole.significato: pitchfork (a large fork used e.g. to move large quantities of hay)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tiugha, tiuva, from Old Norse tjúga, from Proto-Germanic *teuhaną (verb). Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk tjuge, Danish høtyv.
From Old Swedish tiughu, from Old Norse tuttugu, from Proto-Germanic *twai tigiwiz.

parole.significato: a bull ((adult) uncastrated male of cattle)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þiūr, from Old Norse þjórr (“bull”), from Proto-Germanic *þeuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)táwros, *(s)téh₂wros (“bison, bull”).

parole.significato: to charm (so as to (try to) make enchanted, romantically or otherwise)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish kiusa, from Old Norse kjósa, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to taste, choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwseti, from *ǵews- (“to taste, try”). Cognate to English choose. The spelling is unetymological and was changed in the 17th century. A modern spelling kjusa would otherwise be

parole.significato: to make a piercing, high-pitched sound; to howl, to screech, to wail, to cry, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þiuta, from Old Norse þjóta, from Proto-Germanic *þeutaną. Cognate with Icelandic þjóta, Norwegian Bokmål tyte, Old English þēotan, Old High German dioȥan.

parole.significato: a thief (one who carries out theft)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þiūver, from Old Norse þjófr, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.
From Old Swedish tiæld, from Old Norse tjald; doublet of tält (“tent.”).
From Old Swedish þiǣna, þiāna, þiēna, from Old Norse þjóna, þéna. Akin to German dienen.

parole.significato: tar (fluid derived from resin in pine wood)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tiæra, from Old Norse tjara, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *terwą. Cognate with Danish tjære, Norwegian tjære, Icelandic tjara, Faroese tjøra, Dutch teer, German Teer and English tar. Also cognate with Finnish terva, Estonian tõrv and Northern Sami darvi. Doublet of töre.

parole.significato: a small forest lake, a forest pond
parole.testo: From Old Norse tjǫrn. Cognate with English tarn.
From Old Swedish tolf, from Old Norse tolf, Runic Swedish ᛐᚢᛆᛚᚠ (tualf), from Proto-Germanic *twalif. Compare Norwegian and Danish tolv, Faroese tólv, Icelandic tólf.
From Old Norse tómr, from Proto-Germanic *tōmaz (“empty”).

parole.significato: a top, a peak (topmost or highest part)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish topper, tupper, from Old Norse toppr, from Proto-Germanic *tuppaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dumb- (“tail, rod, staff, pole, penis”).

parole.significato: should (be) and also probably is; auxiliary verb used to express probable, but still hypothetical, actions or condition…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þora, þøra, from Old Norse þora, of unknown origin. Doublet of töras ("to dare").

parole.significato: a geotrupid (any beetle in the family Geotrupidae); an earth-boring dung beetle, a dorbeetle
parole.testo: From Old Norse torðýfill. Cognate with Old English tordwifel and Norwegian Nynorsk tordivel.

parole.significato: The letter "T" in the Swedish spelling alphabet
parole.testo: From Old Norse Þórir.

Equivalent to torft + -ig, from Old Swedish thorftogher, thørftugher, from Old Norse þurftugr, from Proto-Germanic *þurftiz. Cognate of Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌿𐍂𐍆𐍄𐍃 (þaurfts), Old Saxon thurftig, German dürftig. Doublet of tarvlig.
From Old Norse torg, from Old East Slavic търгъ (tŭrgŭ, “trade, trading, commerce; (trade) square”), from Proto-Slavic *tъrgъ. Cognate with Danish torv and Icelandic torg (“a square”).
From Old Norse turn, from Middle Low German tōrn, tōren, from Old French tor, from Latin turris, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis), τύρσις (túrsis), from a Mediterranean substrate loan.
From Old Swedish þorn, from Old Norse þorn, from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz, whence also Old English þorn (English thorn). From Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós from *(s)ter- (“stiff”).

parole.significato: A solitary farm, distant from other settlements.
parole.testo: From Old Norse þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą, whence also with German Dorf and Dutch dorp.
From Old Norse þurr, from Proto-Germanic *þursuz, from Proto-Indo-European *térsus, from *ters- (“dry”).

parole.significato: Thursday (now generally considered the fourth day of the week in non-religious contexts in Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þórsdagr, from Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”), calque of Latin dies Iovis.
From Old Swedish þorsker, from Old Norse þorskr, from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz.
From Old Swedish torf, törf, from Old Norse torf, from Proto-Germanic *turbz (“turf, lawn”), from Proto-Indo-European *dorbh- (“tuft, grass”).

parole.significato: rolag, cohesive smaller mass of wool or linen and the like
parole.testo: From Old Norse þáttr, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtu-, from Proto-Indo-European *tonk-tu-. According to Pokorny, this is related to *tek- (“to weave, to plait”), see also Latin texō (“to weave”), Old High German dūhen (“to press”).

From Old Swedish trampa, from Old Norse trampa, from Proto-Germanic *trampaną, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *drem- (“to run”). Cognate with Norwegian trampe. Compare English trample. The noun is derived from the verb.
From Old Norse trana.
From Old Norse þrǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *þrastuz, from Proto-Indo-European *trosdos.

From Old Swedish þrir, þrī, from Runic Swedish þrīR, from Old Norse þrír, from Proto-Norse ᚦᚱᛁᛃᛟᛉ (þrijoʀ) (feminine plural), from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Norwegian and Danish tre, Icelandic þrír, Faroese tríggir.
From Old Swedish þriþi (later tridhie), from Old Norse þriði, from Proto-Germanic *þridjô.
Old Swedish þryzker, from Old Norse þrjózkr (“defiant”). Compare Icelandic þrjóskur (“stubborn”).
From Old Swedish þryzka, from Old Norse þrjózka. Compare Icelandic þrjóska (“stubbornness”).
tre + -faldig, from Old Swedish þrefaldugher, from Old Norse þrēfaldr, from Proto-Germanic *þrifalþaz.
From Old Swedish þrættan, from Old Norse þrettán, from Proto-Germanic *þritehun.
Inherited from Old Swedish thriva, further origin uncertain; perhaps an expressive derivation from Old Norse þrífa (“to seize, grab, snatch”).

parole.significato: nice and pleasant towards others, personable
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þriflika, from Old Norse þrifligr. Cognate with Norwegian trivelig. Equivalent to trivas + -lig.

parole.significato: To feel a durable sense of comfort and satisfaction.
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þrīvas ("to go forward; to grow; to be strengthened; to be successful"), from Old Norse þrífast (“to thrive”), from Proto-Germanic *þrībaną. Related to English thrive and thrift. See also trivsel.

parole.significato: belief (that something is true or real (without being perfectly certain))
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trō, from Old Norse trú, from Proto-Germanic *trewwō.

parole.significato: to believe, (in the sense of "to believe") to think (think that something is true or real (without being perfectly cert…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish trōa, trōa, from Old Norse trúa, from Proto-Germanic *trūwāną.
From Old Norse trǫll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą, from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂-.

parole.significato: to persistently urge or attempt to persuade someone to accept an offering, particularly of food or drink; to urge, to p…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish þruga (“threaten; force; urge someone to”), from Old Norse þrúga (“threaten, force”). Etymologically related to trycka (“to push”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk truga (“threaten”) and Danish true (“threaten”).

parole.significato: any of several species of large gulls with a red spot on the lower mandible
parole.testo: From Old Swedish thrutin, from Old Norse þrútna. Cognate with English throat (from Old English þrote).
From Old Swedish þrykkia, from Old Norse þrykkja, from Proto-Germanic *þrukkijaną.

parole.significato: a snowshoe (usually for a horse, but some types can be used for humans)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse [Term?]. Compare Icelandic þrúga f (“human snowshoe”), Old Norse þrjúgr m and Norwegian Nynorsk truge f (“human snowshoe”). The Norwegian word in some areas had original use as the Swedish one, but now means a snowshoe made for humans (not horses). May be related to English
From Old Norse tryggr, from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz.
From Old Norse trýni.

parole.significato: to (begin to) run out (of supplies, time, patience)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þrȳta, from Old Norse þrjóta, from Proto-Germanic *þreutaną.
From Old Swedish thrækker, from Old Norse þrekkr, from Proto-Germanic *þrakjaz.

From Old Swedish trǣet, trǣt, later trǣdh, originally the definite form of trǣ (“tree, wood”), from Old Norse tré, from Proto-Germanic *trewą (“tree, wood”), from pre-Germanic *dréwom, thematic e-grade derivative of Proto-Indo-European *dóru (“tree”). Doublet of trä. The form trædh, trädh was used s

Uncertain. Possibly past participle of träga (“bereave”). Compare Old English trega, tregian, Icelandic trega, tregi. Possibly derived from Old Norse tregr. Compare origin of Danish træg, German träge.

From Old Swedish þræl, from Old Norse þræll, from Proto-Germanic *þragilaz, *þrahilaz, *þrēhilaz, from the root *þreh-, *þreg-, *þrag- ‘to run’, from Proto-Indo-European *trāgʰ- (“pull, drag, race, run”).
Inherited from Old Swedish thräla, from Old Norse þræla, equivalent to träl + -a. Cognate of Danish trælle and English thrall (“enslave”).
From Old Norse þrældómr (“thralldom”). By surface analysis, träl + -dom. Akin to Danish trældom, Norwegian Bokmål trelldom. Compare English thralldom.

parole.significato: to press, to push, to cram
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þrængia, from Old Norse þrøngva, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwijaną (“to press, to push”). See Danish trenge, Norwegian Bokmål trenge, Norwegian Nynorsk trenga, Icelandic þröngva.
From Old Norse þrá, from Proto-Germanic *þrawō (“longing, suffering”).
From Old Norse þráðr (“thread”), from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *treh₁-tu-, from *terh₁- (“rub, twist”). Definition 3 is probably a calque of English thread.
From Old Norse trog, from Proto-Germanic *trugaz. Cognate of German Trog, Norwegian Nynorsk trau, Icelandic trog, Dutch trog and English trough.

parole.significato: tight, narrow, cramped (not able to comfortably accommodate someone/something)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þranger, from Old Norse þrǫngr, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from *þrinhwaną (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to push, press”). Cognate with English throng, Icelandic þröngur, Nynorsk trong, German dringen.
From Old Swedish trögher, ultimately from the root of Old Norse trauðr (“unwilling, reluctant”).
From Old Swedish þriska, from Old Norse þreskja, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub”).

parole.significato: a threshold, a door sill, a barrier

From Old Norse traust, from Proto-Germanic *traustą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *derw-, *drew-, *drū-.

From Old Norse tvau, neuter nominative/accusative of tveir.

From Old Norse tullr, from Proto-Germanic *tullaz (“toll, custom”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol- (“calculation, fraud”).
From Old Swedish þumi, from Old Norse þúmi, from Proto-Germanic *þūmô (“thumb”).

From Old Norse þunnr, from Proto-Germanic *þunnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ténh₂us.

From Old Norse tveim.
From Old Swedish tvænne, from Old Norse tvennir, from Proto-Germanic *twinaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.

Inherited from Old Swedish thvīna, from Old Norse þvína, from Proto-Germanic *þwīnaną. Cognate of English dwindle.
From Old Swedish þvinga, from Old Norse þvinga, from Proto-Germanic *þwinganą. Related to Proto-Germanic *þwangiz (“pressure, restraint, clamp, strap”). Cognates: see zwingen.

parole.significato: (often with a particle like ihop (“together”), samman (“together”), or upp (“up (untwist)”)) to twist, to twine (thread…

parole.significato: across, perpendicular to the main direction
parole.testo: From Old Swedish þvar, þvær, from Old Norse þverr, from Proto-Germanic *þwerhaz, presumably from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ-.

parole.significato: laundry (clothes and linen to be washed or newly washed)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þváttr, from Proto-Germanic *þwahtuz. Related to två.

From Old Swedish þvā, from Old Norse þvá, from Proto-Germanic *þwahaną.

From Old Swedish þy, from Old Norse því, dative singular of Old Norse þat (“that”).

parole.significato: to cling to, to turn to [someone/something] for protection or comfort.

parole.significato: to be of the opinion (subjectively or objectively), to think

parole.significato: to interpret; to understand the meaning of

parole.significato: German (of or pertaining to Germany, Germans, or the German language)

From Old Norse þekkr.

parole.significato: to tell, to recount, to count

From Old Swedish tæmia, from Old Norse temja, from Proto-Germanic *tamjaną.

parole.significato: to stretch (make longer or more spacious (by pulling or stretching))

parole.significato: a girl or young woman, a maiden, especially a handmaiden or maid

From Old Norse þéttr (“tight, watertight”), from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz. Doublet of tajt.

parole.significato: to compete, to contend, to race

parole.significato: to be able to tolerate, to stand, to bear, to endure (without becoming angry, sick, or sad or giving up or the like)

parole.significato: a tear (drop of clear salty liquid from the eyes)

From Old Swedish tø̄ma, from Old Norse tœma, from Proto-Germanic *tōmijaną.

Inherited from Old Swedish þørster, þorster, from Old Norse þyrstr, from Proto-Germanic *þurstiz, *þurstuz.

From Late Modern Swedish ugla, from Old Swedish uggla, from Old Norse ugla, from Proto-Germanic *uwwulǭ (“owl”). Feminine in Late Modern Swedish. Akin to English owl.

From Old Norse ór, úr, from Proto-Germanic *uz.

From Old Norse val (related to the verb velja (“to choose”)), from Proto-Germanic *walą. Related to välja, vilja (English will).

From Old Swedish ǣgha, from Old Norse eiga, from Proto-Germanic *aiganą, from Proto-Indo-European *eik-.

parole.testo: From Old Swedish æg, from Old Norse egg, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm.

parole.significato: to engage oneself (in some activity), to spend time (doing something)
parole.testo: From Old Norse eigna, related to eiginn. Related to äga (“to own”) and egen (“(one's) own”). Also compare German eignen, English own.
Equivalent to äga + -o- + del, from Old Swedish æghodel, from Old Norse eigudeill. Cognate of Danish ejendel, Norwegian eiendel.
From Old Swedish ælgher, from Old Norse elgr, from Proto-Germanic *algiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁élḱis, *h₁ólḱis.

parole.significato: to love (romantically or otherwise – same tone as in English)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ælska, from Old Norse ælska (Compare Old West Norse elska). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *aliskōną (“to care for, cultivate, cherish”).
Inherited from Old Swedish ælskeliker, from Old Norse elskuligr, equivalent to älska + -lig. Cognate with Danish elskelig.

parole.significato: General term for several child diseases, especially the rickets.
parole.testo: According to Nationalencyklopedins ordbok, the noun definition is attested since 1635, originally meaning "something". The verb comes from the Old Swedish ælta (“to drive, to hunt; to stir, to knead”), from Old Norse elta (“to drive, hunt, knead”), akin to Norwegian Bokmål elte, from Proto-Germanic
From Old Norse elfr, from Proto-Germanic *albī (“river”). Compare Norwegian Bokmål elv, German Elbe.

parole.significato: A human-like creature from Swedish mythology similar to a fairy or elf. She is often a young beautiful female, and can…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ælf, from Old Norse alfr, from Proto-Germanic *albiz (“fairy, elf”).

From Old Swedish æmbete, æmbite, æmbit, æmbeti, from Old Norse embætti, from Proto-Germanic *ambahtiją, whence also ambassad (“embassy”), ambassadör (“ambassador”), amt (“county in Denmark”), German Amt, and Finnish ammatti.
From Old Norse efna, from Proto-Germanic *abnijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃op-, *h₃ep-.
From Old Swedish æfni, from Old Norse efni, from Proto-Germanic *abniją.
From Old Norse enn, from Proto-Germanic *andi, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entí.
From Old Norse an, from earlier *þan, from Proto-Germanic *þan. Cognate with English than.
From the oblique case of ände, from Old Swedish ænde, from Old Norse endi, endir, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz.
From Old Swedish ænda, from Old Norse enda, from Proto-Germanic *andijōną.

parole.significato: an end (of some series of events)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ændalykt, from Old Norse endalykt, equivalent to ända + lykt. Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk endelykt.
From Old Norse endir, from Proto-Germanic *andijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂entíos.
From Old Norse endaþarmr, from endi + þarmr.

parole.significato: a meadow, a field of grass
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æng, from Old Norse eng, from Proto-Germanic *angijō.
From Old Swedish ængil, from Old Norse engill, ultimately from Koine Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).

parole.significato: a widow (a woman whose husband has died)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ænkia, from Old Norse ekkja (Old East Norse ænkja), from Proto-Germanic *ainakjǭ.
From Old Norse enni, from Proto-Germanic *anþiją.
From Old Norse epli, from Proto-Germanic *apaliją, *apluz (“apple, fruit”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.

parole.significato: a matter, an errand (purpose of a small trip), an issue, a task, a work item (in a workflow)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ærande, ærinde, ærende, from Old Norse erendi, ørendi, eyrendi (“errand”), from Proto-Germanic *airundiją. Cognate with Danish ærinde, Norwegian ærend, dialectal German Erend and English errand.
From Old Swedish æria, from Old Norse erja, from Proto-Germanic *arjaną.
From Old Swedish ærke-, from Old Norse erki-, from Old English ærce-, from Latin archi-, from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-).

parole.significato: sleeve; a part of a garment that covers all or part of an arm
parole.testo: From Old Norse ermr, from Proto-Germanic *armijō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erm-i(e)h₂-. See *armaz.

parole.significato: scar (a permanent mark on the skin sometimes caused by the healing of a wound)
parole.testo: From Old Norse ørr, from Proto-Germanic *arwaz.

parole.significato: Any species in the Fabacea family
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ært f, from Old Norse ertr, from Old Saxon erit, eriwit, from Proto-Germanic *arwīts. Cognates include Danish ært, Faroese ertur, Norwegian ert, Dutch erwt and German Erbse. Possibly related to Latin ervum and Ancient Greek ὄροβος (órobos).
From Old Swedish ærva, from Old Norse erfa, from Proto-Germanic *arbijaną, equivalent to arv + -a.

parole.significato: box made out of heat-bent wood
parole.testo: From dialectal äska ("little box"), from ask (“box”), from Old Swedish asker, from Old Norse askr, from Proto-Germanic *askaz.

parole.significato: a forge, a furnace, a hearth (a place for heating metal in a blacksmith's shop)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æsia, from Old Norse esja, from Proto-Germanic *asjǭ.
From Old Swedish æta, from Old Norse eta, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-.

parole.significato: a (noble or royal) family, a house
parole.testo: From Old Swedish æt, from Old Norse ætt, from Proto-Germanic *aihtiz.

parole.significato: a high steep inland cliff from which the elderly in Nordic antiquity were said to have thrown themselves, or been throw…
parole.testo: Compound of ätt (“kin, clan”) + stupa (“precipice”). Possibly folk etymology of Old Norse Ætternisstapi (“The Dynasty Precipice”), a fictional cliffside in Gautreks saga, similar to one mentioned by Pliny the Elder and other ancient authors, and common in many legends worldwide. First time used in 1

parole.significato: Various concentrations of acetic acid; white vinegar.
parole.testo: From late Old Norse edik, from Middle Low German etik or Middle Dutch edik, from Proto-West Germanic *atek, metathesized variant of *aket, from Latin acētum. parole.significato: an adventure (unusual, exciting (and dangerous) undertaking or experience)
parole.testo: From late Old Norse æfintýr, from Middle Low German eventü̂r, from Middle French adventure (“aventure”).
From Old Swedish æfia (“mud”), from Old Norse efja, from Proto-Germanic *abjǭ (“ebb”). Cognate with Icelandic efja.

parole.significato: a river, a creek, a big stream
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ā, from Old Norse á, from Proto-Germanic *ahwō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂.
From Old Norse á, from Proto-Germanic *ana.
From Old Swedish aþra/adher (Old Norse æðr), from Proto-Germanic *ēþrǭ. Cognate with Old English ǣdre, Danish åre, Norwegian åre, German Ader and Dutch ader.
From Old Swedish aþra, adher, from Old Norse æðr, from Proto-Germanic *ēþrō. Cognate with Old English ǣdre, Danish åre, Norwegian åre, German Ader and Dutch ader.
From Old Norse ó, which was used in the same way as åh is today.

parole.significato: to go by using something more or other than the human or animal body, for example a vehicle, skis, or skates; to go, to…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish aka, from Old Norse aka, from Proto-Germanic *akaną. Cognate with Danish age. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eǵ-. Doublet of agera, which was borrowed from Latin agō, from the same ultimate Proto-Indo-European source.

parole.significato: The letter "Å" in the Swedish spelling alphabet
parole.testo: From Old Norse Áki, diminutive of Proto-Norse *ᚨᚾᚢᛉ (*anuʀ, “ancestor”), from Proto-Germanic *anô (as in the first part of the name Olaf). By folk etymology sometimes associated with Swedish åka (“ride”), as in Åke-Tor, an epithet of the thunder god Thor. Formerly an eastern Danish name (in what is

parole.significato: field; a wide, open space that is used to grow crops
parole.testo: From Old Swedish aker, from Old Norse akr, from Proto-Germanic *akraz (“field”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros (“field”). Akin to English acre.
From Old Swedish āl, from Old Norse áll, from Proto-Germanic *ēlaz.

parole.significato: age; how old something or someone is
parole.testo: From Old Swedish alder, from Old Norse aldr, from Proto-Germanic *aldrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- (“to grow”).

parole.significato: to impose a formal requirement (on someone, to do or not do something); to impose, to prescribe, (of a punishment) to i…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish ālæggia, from Old Norse leggja á, from Proto-Germanic *analagjaną. Equivalent to å (“on (obsolete)”) + lägga (“lay”). Cognate with German anlegen, English onlay.
From Old Swedish anger, from Old Norse angr, from Proto-Germanic *angazaz. Compare English anger.
From Old Swedish anger, from Old Norse angr. Likely influenced by Old West Norse.
From Old Norse angist or ángist.
From Old Swedish angra, from Old Norse angra (“to grieve, to vex, to distress”), equivalent to ånger + -a. Compare Danish angre, Norwegian angre, English anger.
From Old Swedish ār, from Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *jērą, from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁r-.
From Old Norse ár, from Proto-Germanic *airō (“oar”). Cognate with Finnish airo.
From Old Swedish aratal, from Old Norse áratal; år + -a- + tal.

parole.significato: an ard, an ard plough, a scratch plough
parole.testo: From Old Swedish arþer, from Old Norse arðr, from Proto-Germanic *arþrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom. Cognate with Icelandic arðr, and Danish, Norwegian, and English ard.
From Old Swedish artal, from Old Norse ártal; år + -a- + tal.

parole.significato: a ridge (long, narrow, not too tall elevation in the landscape)
parole.testo: From Old Norse áss (“rocky ridge”), from Proto-Germanic *amsaz (“shoulder”).
Inherited from Old Norse asni, borrowed from Old French asne, from Latin asinus.
From Old Norse at, from Proto-Germanic *at, from Proto-Indo-European *ád.
From Old Norse atburðr.
From Old Swedish āter, from Old Norse aptr, from Proto-Germanic *aftrą.

parole.significato: an action, a measure (aiming to achieve a result)
parole.testo: Compound of åt (“at”) + gärd (“act, action”); from Old Swedish ātgærþ, from Old Norse atgerð. Compare Icelandic aðgerð, Norwegian åtgjerd. Directly related is the verb åtgärda (the act of åtgärd), from åtgöra (“to do, to carry out”), from Old Swedish ātgø̄ra.
From Old Swedish ātta, āta, from Old Norse átta, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Icelandic átta, Norwegian åtte, Danish otte.
From Old Swedish āttande, āttunde, from Old Norse áttundi, by analogy from earlier átti, from Proto-Germanic *ahtudô.

parole.significato: island, isle (piece of land surrounded by water)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Swedish ø, from Old Norse ey, from Proto-Germanic *awjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ekʷeh₂ (“water”). Cognate with Swedish å (“stream”), English ey (and the initial syllable in island).

parole.significato: to waste, to spend in vain, often used about time
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄þa, from Old Norse eyða, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaną. Cognate with Icelandic eyða, Danish øde, German veröden. Based on the adjective öde (“waste, desolate”) from Old Swedish ø̄þe = Danish øde, Old Saxon ôthi, Old High German ôdi (“empty”), Old Norse auðr (“desolate”).

parole.significato: deserted, desolate, empty (void of people or human activity)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄þe, from Old Norse auðr, from Proto-Germanic *auþijaz.

From phrases of the type det är ödet, where the word has been reinterpreted as the definite article of a neuter noun öde, but is originally the neuter of an obsolete adjective öden, from Old Swedish ø̄þen, from Old Norse auðinn 'destined, fallen to one's lot, granted', formally a participle of an ob
From Old Norse eðla, eyðla, øðla.
From Old Swedish ø̄gha, from Old Norse auga, from Proto-Germanic *augô, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”).

parole.significato: a draught animal or beast of burden
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄ker, from Old Norse eykr.
From Old Swedish ø̄ka, from Old Norse auka, from Proto-Germanic *aukaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg-. Akin to English eke, Danish øge, Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌺𐌰𐌽 (aukan), Latin augeō.
From Old Swedish öknamn, from Old Norse aukanafn. Equivalent to öka + namn. Cognate with Danish øgenavn, English nickname and Norwegian Nynorsk aukenamn
From Old Swedish ø̄dhkænder‚ from Old Norse auðkendr (“easily known”), from auð- + kenna. Cognate with Danish åkjendt, Norwegian Nynorsk audkjend, and Icelandic auðkenndur (“marked”).

parole.significato: a beer (a kind or brand of beer)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish öl, from Old Norse ǫl (“ale, beer”), from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut- (“beer”), or *h₂elu- (“bitter”). Cognate with Icelandic öl. Probably related to Latin alūmen (“alum”); the meaning of "feast" comes from the custom of beer being served at feasts.
From Old Swedish ømber, from Old Norse aumr, which is related to armr (“poor, unhappy”). Cognate with Danish øm.
From Old Swedish ømka, from Old Norse aumka, equivalent to öm + -ka. Doublet of ynka and ömma. Cognate with Danish ynke.
From Old Swedish ømkan, from Old Norse aumkan.

parole.significato: both (especially of pairs coming from two directions)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ymse, from Old Norse ýmiss.

parole.significato: sometimes, at times, alternately, by turns (in one set of instances (that alternate (and contrast) with other instances…
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ymsom, from ýmsum, dative plural form of Old Norse ýmiss (“various”). Attested in the form umisum on the Rök runestone.
From Old Swedish ȳskia, ø̄skia, from Old Norse œskja (“wish”), from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”). The 'n' stems from influence from Middle Low German wunschen. Compare German wünschen.

From Old Swedish ypin, øppin, from Old Norse opinn, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz. Compare Norwegian open, Danish åben, Icelandic opinn, Dutch open, Low German apen, open, German offen, West Frisian iepen, English open.
From Old Swedish ypna, øpna, from Old Norse opna, öppen + -a.

parole.significato: ear; the part of the body used to hear
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄ra, from Old Norse eyra, from the voiced Verner alternant of Proto-Germanic *ausô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ows-.

parole.significato: a currency unit, one hundredth of a krona (in Denmark, Norway, Sweden)
parole.testo: From Old Norse eyrir, from Proto-Germanic *aurijaz. Potentially related to Latin aureus (“gold coin”), however, according to SAOB not derived from it according to new research. First attested in the 9th to 10th century.

From Old Swedish øridh, from Old Norse aurriði, from aurr (“sandbank”) (from Proto-Germanic *auraz) + a descendant of Proto-Norse [script needed] (*-ræið-, “travel”), a more broad form of rīþa (“ride”) (from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną). -ridh has transformed into the common suffix -ing in modern Swedish

parole.significato: naval, war; pertaining to naval warfare
parole.testo: See örlig (“war”), from Old Norse ørlǫg, from Proto-Germanic *uzlagą. Cognate Dutch oorlog (“war”).
From Old Norse ǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *arô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃or-no- (“eagle”).

From Old Norse urt, oblique case form of Proto-Germanic *wrōts, from Proto-Indo-European *wrd- (“root”). Compare with English wort and the Latin rādīx (“root”). Cognate with the Icelandic rót; Old English rōt (whence Middle English root (“the underground part of a plant”), whence English root).

parole.significato: to scoop (move a fluid, one scoop at a time), pour, serve
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄sa, from Old Norse ausa, from Proto-Germanic *ausaną.
From Old Norse austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą.

parole.significato: The letter "Ö" in the Swedish spelling alphabet
parole.testo: From Old Norse Eysteinn (compare Norwegian Øystein), from ey (“luck”) + steinn (“stone”).

parole.significato: east; one of the four major compass points
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ø̄ster, from Old Norse austr, from Proto-Germanic *austrą.
From Old Swedish ivir, yvir, ø̄wer, from Runic Swedish ufiR, from Old Norse yfir, from Proto-Germanic *ubiri, from Proto-Indo-European *upéri, from *upér, from *upo.
From Old Swedish yver, from Old Norse yfir.

parole.significato: excessive violence (more violence than is necessary)
parole.testo: From Old Swedish ivirvald, from Old Norse yfirvald, equivalent to över (“over”) + våld (“violence”). Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål overvold, Danish overvold, Icelandic yfirvald (“authority”), German Obergewalt (“supremacy”).
From Old Norse øfri, efri.
